hamper|sc2.stem: Wearing a cast on her right wrist did not stop Ava from finishing the art project, but it did _____ her, so she needed twice as long to draw each line.

decoys.why: The cast made her need twice as long, so it did not make her stronger.
Needing twice as long to draw each line is a problem, not a comfort.
A cast slowing her drawing is no special pleasure for Ava.
The cast did not attract her with anything; it slowed her down.
A cast cannot say the opposite of anything; it made her drawing slower.

impeccable|sc1.stem: The gymnast's routine was _____; the judges could not find a single wobble or misstep, and all five awarded her a perfect ten.

decoys.why: The judges found no wobble at all, so the routine was not shaky.
A perfect ten with no misstep means calm control, not wild hurry.
A routine earning five perfect tens is far from ordinary and dull.
The judges gave perfect scores, so the routine was not laughably silly.
A gymnastics routine is full of motion, and the clue is about having no flaws.

impeccable|sc2.stem: Although Marcus usually rushed through his chores, the day before his grandparents' visit he left his bedroom _____, with every shirt folded and not a speck of dust anywhere.

decoys.why: The sentence says this time he did not rush, leaving the room carefully finished.
Folded shirts and no dust describe a flawless room, not fancy decorations.
A room is not flowing water; the clue is folded shirts and no dust.
The sentence stresses how unusually perfect the room was, not how ordinary.
Nothing was about to fall; every shirt was folded and the room was spotless.

prodigy|sc1.stem: By age seven, Mei could play difficult Mozart sonatas that many adult pianists struggled with, so newspapers began calling her a musical _____.

decoys.why: Mei really could play hard Mozart sonatas, so she was no trick.
Nothing says Mei did what she told others not to do.
Playing music adults struggle with is impressive, not a foolish act.
Newspapers were praising her talent, not describing a painful experience.
Her skill was real, so it was not a mistaken belief.
Her talent was genuine, not a false appearance hiding something.

prodigy|sc2.stem: Though he was only ten and still needed a booster seat in the car, Ethan was a math _____ who solved college problems that stumped his older cousins.

decoys.why: Ethan is praised for solving hard problems, not for doing what he tells others not to.

conscientious|sc1.stem: Unlike her careless lab partner, Priya was _____, double-checking every measurement and recording each result neatly before moving on.

decoys.why: Priya double-checked every measurement, so she was very aware of what she was doing.
Careful checking and neat records show she took the work seriously.
Double-checking everything before moving on is calm and careful, not wild hurry.
Nothing shows Priya being annoying; she is praised for being careful.
Her results were recorded neatly, so nothing about her was mysterious.

conscientious|sc2.stem: Because Jonah was so _____ about his paper route, wrapping every newspaper in plastic whenever rain was forecast, his customers never once found a soggy paper on their porch.

decoys.why: Jonah checked the forecast and wrapped papers, so he paid close attention.
Wrapping every paper before rain shows he took the job seriously.
Jonah planned ahead calmly, and the sentence shows no wild worry or hurry.
Nothing about his paper route was mysterious; the clue is his careful work.

cryptic|sc1.stem: The treasure hunt clue was so _____ that the campers spent an hour arguing about what "where the sun sleeps twice" could possibly mean.

decoys.why: The campers argued an hour over its meaning, so the clue was not plain.
The clue is short, and the problem was its meaning, not its size.
The campers argued about what it meant, not about how clean it was.
A puzzling clue is confusing, not fierce.
A clue does not flow or grow; the campers could not understand it.

cryptic|sc2.stem: Most of Grandpa's text messages are long and clear, but last night he sent a _____ one that said only "Owl. Blue door. Noon?" leaving everyone confused.

decoys.why: This message was only four words, so it was not long or bulky.
Everyone was confused by the text, so its meaning was not easy to see.
The sentence is about the message confusing everyone, not about it being clean.
Nothing in the short text was fierce; it was just puzzling.
A text message does not flow or grow; it was simply hard to understand.

aptitude|sc1.stem: Even as a toddler, Hiro had a remarkable _____ for music; he could pick out songs on the piano before anyone had taught him a single note.

decoys.why: Hiro loved picking out songs on his own, so he did not look down on music.
Nothing in the sentence shows Hiro hated music; he played it eagerly before any lessons.

aptitude|sc2.stem: Although my brother practiced soccer every single day, he never showed much _____ for it, while his little sister scored three goals in her very first game.

decoys.why: He practiced every day, so he did not scorn soccer; the contrast is about natural skill.
The sentence compares his skill with his sister's goals, not whether he hated soccer.

deprive|sc1.stem: Building the parking lot would _____ the neighborhood's children of their only park, leaving them nowhere safe to play.

decoys.why: Leaving children nowhere safe to play would worry them, not comfort them.

deprive|sc2.stem: The long drought would _____ the farm's thirsty crops of water, taking away the one thing they needed most to grow.

decoys.why: A drought takes water away from crops; it does not comfort them about anything.

ornate|sc1.stem: Unlike the plain modern buildings around it, the old theater was _____, with carved angels, swirling patterns, and gold trim covering every wall.

decoys.why: The clue lists carved angels and gold trim, which is about decoration, not cleanliness.
Nothing suggests the theater might fall; the sentence describes its fancy decoration.
Swirling patterns and gold trim show decoration, not something mysterious or hard to understand.
Stagnant describes still water or no growth, not a building covered in carvings.

ornate|sc2.stem: The jewelry box was so _____ that it took the woodcarver three months to finish all the tiny flowers, vines, and birds on its lid.

decoys.why: Tiny flowers and vines took time because of detail, not because the box was heavy.
Three months of carving tiny flowers points to fancy detail, not clean and untouched.
Being unsafe or likely to fall would not make carving the lid take three months.
The carvings are flowers and birds, so nothing about the box is mysterious.

finesse|sc1.stem: The pastry chef decorated the cake with such _____ that each sugar flower looked delicate and real, as if it had just been picked from a garden.

decoys.why: Flowers that look delicate and real show careful skill, not looking down on the work.
The sentence praises the chef's delicate work and says nothing about pain or sorrow.
Sugar flowers that look real show great skill, the opposite of foolishness.
Decorating delicate sugar flowers shows graceful skill, not hostility toward anyone.

finesse|sc2.stem: While the younger players just kicked the ball as hard as they could, the team captain dribbled past defenders with _____, gently guiding the ball wherever she wanted.

decoys.why: She was gently guiding the ball, which shows graceful control, not hostility.
The captain is calmly controlling the ball, with no sign of pain or sorrow.
Camaraderie is friendship in a group, but the sentence is about her own ball skill.

arduous|sc1.stem: For pioneer families, crossing the Rocky Mountains by wagon was truly _____; they pushed through deep snow, steep trails, and weeks of exhaustion.

decoys.why: Deep snow and weeks of exhaustion make the trip serious, not silly or unimportant.
Pushing through snow and steep trails is hard physical work, not sitting around.
Weeks of exhaustion are nothing playful or fanciful about the journey.
Ornate describes fancy decoration, but the sentence is about a hard, tiring journey.

arduous|sc2.stem: My older sister said the science project would be quick and simple, but it turned out to be _____, keeping us up late gluing and measuring for five nights.

decoys.why: Five late nights of work show the project was hard, not silly or unimportant.
The clue is staying up late for five nights, which points to hard work, not playfulness.
The sentence contrasts quick and simple with long effort, not with how perfect it looked.
The contrast with quick and simple is about effort, not about fancy decoration.

discern|sc1.stem: The two paintings were so alike that only an expert could _____ the tiny differences in brushstrokes that showed which one was the original.

decoys.why: The sentence is about telling the paintings apart, not copying them, so emulate misses the point.
Protecting the paintings is not what the expert does here; the expert notices differences.
Differences in brushstrokes are spotted, not brought to mind like a memory.
The expert uses the differences to find the original, not to wipe them out.
You cannot say the opposite of brushstrokes; the expert must notice them.
The differences are real clues, so the expert would not prove them wrong.

discern|sc2.stem: Through my scratched old glasses, I could barely _____ the words on the board, but with my new pair every letter looks sharp and clear.

decoys.why: The problem is seeing the words through scratched glasses, not copying someone you admire.
The scratched glasses made the words hard to see, not hard to erase.
The sentence is about seeing the words clearly, not arguing against them.
Bad glasses affect how well you see the words, not whether you prove them wrong.
Words on a board are seen, and the new glasses fix seeing, not memory.

frivolous|sc1.stem: Mr. Kim urged the class to spend the fundraiser money on useful supplies like microscopes rather than _____ items such as glitter stickers and party hats.

decoys.why: Glitter stickers and party hats are contrasted with useful supplies, so they are not clever.
Stickers and party hats are not heavy or hard to carry; they are simply unimportant.
Mr. Kim objects that the items are not useful, not that they are perfect.
The contrast is useful versus silly, and being clean has nothing to do with it.
Glitter stickers and party hats are not mysterious; the point is they are not useful.

frivolous|sc2.stem: Grandpa called my plan to buy a light-up hat with my birthday money _____, saying it was a waste spent on something that didn't really matter.

decoys.why: Grandpa called the plan a waste, so he would not praise it as clever.
Grandpa thought the plan was a waste, not careful and responsible.
Grandpa complained the hat didn't matter, not that the plan was risky or unsafe.
Buying a hat is not hard work; Grandpa objected that it was unimportant.
The plan was easy to understand; Grandpa just thought it was a waste.
Calling something a waste is criticism, so Grandpa would not call it perfect.

misconception|sc1.stem: Many people believe that goldfish have only a three-second memory, but this is a common _____; studies show they can remember things for months.

decoys.why: The belief is simply wrong, as studies show, not a true statement that seems contradictory.
The sentence says goldfish memory is actually good, so the issue is a wrong belief, not a shortage.
A facade hides feelings; this sentence is about people believing something untrue.
Nobody is complaining about unfairness; people simply believe something false about goldfish.
The sentence describes a belief that studies proved wrong, not a natural talent.
The goldfish idea is a mistaken belief, not a sign of something to come.

misconception|sc2.stem: Many people hold the _____ that the Great Wall of China can be seen from space, a mistaken idea that astronauts have shown to be false.

decoys.why: The sentence calls it a mistaken idea shown false, not a true statement that seems contradictory.
Seeing the Great Wall from space is a false belief, not a complaint about unfairness.
People believe something about the Great Wall; they do not look down on anything here.
The sentence names a mistaken idea, not a natural ability.
The belief about the Great Wall is a false idea, not a sign of the future.

ferocious|sc1.stem: The usually gentle river became _____ after a week of heavy rain, its roaring brown water tearing whole trees from the banks.

decoys.why: The water was roaring and tearing out trees, so it was moving wildly, not still.
The water was muddy brown and destructive, not clean and untouched.
Sedentary describes sitting people, and this river was roaring and tearing out trees.
A river tearing trees from its banks is fierce, not decorated with fancy detail.
Nothing about the river is mysterious; the clues show it became violent and powerful.

ferocious|sc2.stem: The storm was so _____ that its winds knocked down power lines across town and kept everyone indoors for two days.

decoys.why: Winds strong enough to knock down power lines are not still or motionless.
A storm that kept everyone indoors for days was serious, not silly.
The storm's damage shows it was fierce, not mysterious or hard to understand.
Knocked down power lines show a destructive storm, not a clean, untouched one.
The storm kept people indoors, but the storm itself was violent, not sitting still.

prolong|sc1.stem: Hoping to _____ their visit to the national park, the family called the lodge and asked whether they could stay three more nights.

decoys.why: The family wanted three more nights, so they wanted to extend the visit, not get in its way.
Asking to stay longer shows they wanted the visit to continue, not to block it.
The family asked for more nights, so they were not trying to hold back their visit.
National parks are conserved, but the family wanted their visit to last longer.
Staying three more nights makes a visit longer; it does not bring up a memory.

prolong|sc2.stem: Most of us wanted the boring assembly to end quickly, but the speaker seemed determined to _____ it with one long story after another.

decoys.why: The long stories made the boring assembly worse for the students, not less painful.
Telling one long story after another keeps the assembly going instead of wiping it out.
The speaker kept talking to stretch out the assembly, not to say the opposite of it.
The students found the assembly boring, so the stories made it longer, not attractive.
The clue is that students wanted it to end quickly, so the speaker made it last longer.

animosity|sc1.stem: The two neighbors had argued about the fence for so long that their _____ was obvious; they glared at each other and refused to speak even at the block party.

decoys.why: They glared and refused to speak, so they had no friendly relationship at all.
Neighbors who glare and won't speak share no friendship or trust.
A facade hides feelings, but these neighbors showed their dislike openly by glaring.
The sentence is about how the neighbors feel about each other, not skill or grace.
Glaring and refusing to speak show a feeling, not a natural ability.
Nothing in the sentence is about a gut feeling; it describes open hostility.

animosity|sc2.stem: Although the two soccer captains had been best friends in third grade, a bitter argument over the championship left nothing but _____ between them by eighth grade.

decoys.why: They were friends once, but the bitter argument ended that friendship.

Soccer suggests plans, but a bitter argument leaves bad feelings, not a plan.
A bitter argument leaves bad feelings between people, not skill or grace.
The sentence describes feelings between former friends, not a natural ability.
A bitter argument leaves hostility, not a gut feeling, between the captains.

rapport|sc1.stem: Because Mr. Okafor learned every student's name and asked about their hobbies, he quickly developed a warm _____ with his new class.

decoys.why: Learning names and asking about hobbies builds friendliness, not hostility.
The word warm and his caring questions show he did not look down on students.
A warm connection built by caring questions is harmony, not disagreement.

An aptitude is a personal ability; you cannot develop one with a class.

rapport|sc2.stem: On the first day the new lab partners barely spoke, but by October they shared jokes and finished each other's sentences, showing a strong _____.

decoys.why: Partners who share jokes and finish each other's sentences like each other.
Sharing jokes shows the partners enjoy each other, not that they look down on each other.
Finishing each other's sentences shows harmony, not disagreement.
Jokes and finished sentences show a friendship, not a natural talent for lab work.
Sharing jokes is about friendship, not a careful plan for a goal.
The clues describe a growing friendship, not skill or grace in handling something.

infer|sc1.stem: Seeing muddy paw prints across the kitchen floor and an empty dog bed, Mom was able to _____ that Rex had escaped through the back door.

decoys.why: The paw prints and empty bed support the idea that Rex escaped; they do not disprove it.
Mom used the clues to reach a conclusion, not to say the opposite of one.

infer|sc2.stem: Nobody told Priya about any surprise, but the whispering friends and the cake hidden in the closet let her _____ that a party was coming.

decoys.why: The whispering and hidden cake pointed to a party, so Priya had nothing to disprove.
Priya used the clues to figure out the surprise, not to deny it.

cumbersome|sc1.stem: The old camping tent was so _____ that it took two people to carry it, so the family bought a lightweight one for their hiking trip.

decoys.why: Sedentary describes sitting a lot, not a tent so heavy it takes two people to carry.
Stagnant means not flowing, like still water; it does not mean heavy.
A perfect tent would not be replaced; the family wanted one that was lighter.
Needing two people to carry it is about weight, not about being silly.
The clue is that the tent was heavy, not playful or fanciful.
Nothing says the tent was confusing; the problem was that it was too heavy.

cumbersome|sc2.stem: Grandpa's old laptop was _____; it weighed nearly ten pounds and was so thick that it would not fit in my backpack.

decoys.why: An old laptop might be confusing, but the clues are its weight and thickness.
Weighing ten pounds and not fitting in a backpack are flaws, not perfection.
Stagnant means not flowing or growing; the clues say the laptop was heavy and thick.
Ten pounds and too thick for a backpack describe bulk, not silliness.
The clues describe a heavy, bulky laptop, not a playful one.
Sedentary describes a person who sits a lot, not a heavy, bulky object.

entice|sc1.stem: To _____ more shoppers into the new bookstore, the owner offered free hot chocolate and set out a table of colorful books by the door.

decoys.why: Free hot chocolate draws shoppers in gently; it does not force anyone anywhere.
Incite means stirring people up to trouble, not attracting them with pleasant treats.

entice|sc2.stem: The zookeeper tried shouting and clapping, but nothing worked until she held out a ripe banana to _____ the stubborn monkey down from the tree.

decoys.why: Shouting tried to force the monkey; the banana worked by tempting it instead.

relinquish|sc1.stem: After leading the debate club for three years, Hannah agreed to _____ her role as president so that a younger member could gain experience.

decoys.why: Hannah steps down so a younger member can lead, so she is not making her role last longer.

relinquish|sc2.stem: Although the puppy whined and tugged, Leo refused to _____ his grip on the leash until they had safely crossed the busy street.

decoys.why: Leo holds on until they cross, so refusing to make his grip last longer makes no sense.

A grip on a leash is not a feeling or memory brought to mind.
A grip is not something you fill up again, and Leo is deciding whether to let go.

dispel|sc1.stem: To _____ the rumor that the cafeteria served worm burgers, the cook invited students into the kitchen to watch her prepare lunch.

decoys.why: Showing students the real cooking would calm the rumor, not stir it up.
The cook wants the rumor gone, not to make it last longer.
The cook is ending the rumor, not figuring it out from clues.
Inviting students in removes the rumor rather than bringing it to mind.

dispel|sc2.stem: Though Ava felt nervous about the new school, her friendly locker neighbor helped _____ her worries by inviting her to sit together at lunch.

decoys.why: A friendly invitation would make Ava's worries go away, not last longer.
The neighbor was kind, so she ended Ava's worries instead of bringing them up.
The neighbor's kindness made the worries disappear, not drew them out.
Inviting Ava to lunch would not fill her worries up again.

elicit|sc1.stem: The teacher asked open-ended questions to _____ thoughtful answers from even her quietest students, who rarely spoke in class.

decoys.why: The teacher wants quiet students to speak, so she is not crushing their answers.
Open-ended questions are meant to bring out answers, not block them.
The teacher wants to hear answers, not prove them wrong.
The teacher is trying to get answers from shy students, not block them.

elicit|sc2.stem: No matter how many silly faces Dad made, he could not _____ even a tiny smile from the grumpy baby, who kept frowning.

decoys.why: Dad was trying to get a smile out of the baby, not figure one out from clues.
Dad made silly faces to draw out a smile, not to stop one.
Dad wanted a smile to appear, not to disappear.

jeopardize|sc1.stem: Coach Rivera warned that missing too many practices could _____ Dante's chance of starting in the championship game.

decoys.why: Missing practices is a warning sign, so it would not fill up Dante's chance.
The coach is warning about a danger, not something that makes Dante's chance last longer.
Missing practice does not reveal a secret, it puts Dante's spot at risk.
A chance is not a statement that can be proved wrong.

jeopardize|sc2.stem: Smart hikers stay on marked trails, but a few careless ones wander off and _____ their own safety by getting lost in the woods.

decoys.why: Getting lost in the woods hurts their safety, so it does not fill it back up.
Careless hikers who get lost are risking their safety, not making it last longer.
The hikers are not revealing secrets, they are putting themselves at risk.
Getting lost does not mean noticing safety, it means endangering it.

whimsical|sc1.stem: The children's book was full of _____ drawings, like pigs with butterfly wings and teapots that danced on tiny legs.

decoys.why: Pigs with butterfly wings are playful and odd, not covered in fancy detail.
Dancing teapots are silly and fanciful, not mysterious or hard to understand.
Pigs with butterfly wings and dancing teapots sound playful, not fierce.

whimsical|sc2.stem: Grandma's living room was plain and serious, but her backyard was totally _____, with flamingo statues wearing sunglasses and a birdbath shaped like a giant teacup.

decoys.why: The backyard is the opposite of serious, and flamingos in sunglasses are playful, not loyal.
A teacup birdbath is fun and odd, not mysterious or hard to understand.
The sentence describes playful decorations, not a yard where people mostly sit.
The but contrasts the backyard with the serious room, so it should sound playful.

mediate|sc1.stem: When the two lab partners could not agree on how to split the work, they asked their teacher to _____ and help them find a fair solution.

decoys.why: The partners wanted a fair solution, and striking back would only make the fight worse.
The teacher was asked to help find a fair solution, not to stir up more trouble.
The teacher was supposed to help them agree, not block their progress.
They wanted the disagreement settled, not made to last longer.

mediate|sc2.stem: Instead of taking sides when her twin brothers fought over the video game controller, Mom sat between them and tried to _____ until they agreed to share turns.

decoys.why: Mom was not taking sides; striking back would not get the twins to share turns.

inept|sc1.stem: Unlike his sister, who could fix any bike, Jonah was so _____ with tools that he once loosened the wrong bolt and the wheel fell off.

decoys.why: Jonah loosened the wrong bolt, so he was clumsy, not skilled.

Loosening the wrong bolt shows Jonah was not sharp with tools at all.

inept|sc2.stem: Because the new goalie was so _____, the other team scored six easy goals before halftime, and the coach finally sent in a backup.

decoys.why: Six easy goals got past him, so the goalie was not skilled.
A flawless goalie would not let in six easy goals and get replaced.

A sharp goalie would stop easy shots, but this one let six in.
Loyalty has nothing to do with letting in six easy goals.

resolute|sc1.stem: Even after failing her driving test twice, Isabel remained _____, signing up for a third attempt the very next morning and practicing every day until she passed.

decoys.why: She failed twice, but signing up again and practicing daily shows determination, not clumsiness.

resolute|sc2.stem: Mia was _____ about learning the hard piano piece; no matter how many wrong notes she hit, she refused to quit and kept practicing every single night.

decoys.why: The piece was difficult, but the blank describes Mia, who refused to quit.
She hit wrong notes, but the clue is that she refused to quit.
Practicing every single night shows she was serious, not silly.
She kept hitting wrong notes, so she was not yet skilled; she was determined.
Refusing to quit and practicing nightly shows firm determination, not playfulness.

incite|sc1.stem: The prankster's fake fire alarm did more than annoy people; it helped _____ panic, sending shoppers rushing for the exits.

decoys.why: Shoppers rushed for the exits, so the alarm caused panic rather than making it disappear.
The alarm sent people rushing out, so it started panic instead of wiping it out.
The alarm did not slow panic; it set off a rush for the exits.
Shoppers rushing out shows the panic grew, not that it was held back.
The exits come up, but the alarm stirred up panic, not blocked anything.

incite|sc2.stem: Instead of calming the angry fans after the referee's bad call, the team's mascot waved his arms and booed, which only seemed to _____ them further.

decoys.why: The sentence says he did not calm the fans, so he did not reassure them.

Waving and booing made the fans angrier, not slowed them down.
The mascot's booing worked them up more, which is the opposite of holding them back.
The mascot was not proving anyone wrong; he was making the fans angrier.

omen|sc1.stem: Ancient sailors believed that a seagull landing on the ship's mast was a lucky _____ that meant calm seas lay ahead.

decoys.why: The sailors believed in the sign, so they would not call it a mistaken belief.
The seagull meant calm seas lay ahead, so it was a sign, not a show of respect.
The seagull did not give help; it was a sign of what was coming.
A seagull that predicts calm seas is a sign, not a talented young person.

omen|sc2.stem: Grandpa laughed when Lucy called the broken mirror a bad _____; he said shattered glass could not predict anything, so she should just sweep it up.

decoys.why: Grandpa thinks it is a mistaken belief, but Lucy called the mirror a sign of bad luck.

The clue is that glass cannot predict anything, so Lucy saw it as a sign.

grievance|sc1.stem: The students brought their _____ to the principal, explaining that it was unfair that only seniors were allowed to use the new gym.

decoys.why: The students are calling something unfair, which is a complaint, not a show of respect.

grievance|sc2.stem: Instead of grumbling in the hallway, the eighth graders wrote down their _____ about the short lunch period and politely asked the student council for a fix.

decoys.why: They are unhappy about a short lunch, so they wrote a complaint, not praise.
The sentence says they asked politely, so they were not writing down hostility.
They politely asked for a fix, which does not match looking down on others.
They are complaining about lunch, not describing friendship within their group.
You cannot write down a friendly relationship about a short lunch period.
A short lunch is a fair complaint, not severe pain or great sorrow.

impede|sc1.stem: A lack of money continued to _____ progress on the new library, which sat half-built for more than a year.

decoys.why: The library sat half-built, so lack of money blocked progress rather than strengthening it.
Lack of money stopped the work, so it did not stir up progress.

Lack of money does not attract progress; the library stayed half-built.

impede|sc2.stem: The new hallway rule was meant to speed up class changes, but instead the crowded single staircase seemed to _____ every student trying to reach class on time.

decoys.why: The crowded staircase made students late, so it did not support or help them.

The sentence is about slowing students down, not stirring them up to act.

steadfast|sc1.stem: Through every losing season, the team's _____ fans never stopped buying tickets, showing up in the rain to cheer as loudly as ever.

decoys.why: Fans who show up in the rain every season are serious, not silly.

The clue is that they never stopped coming, not that they sat a lot.

steadfast|sc2.stem: Most of the kids quit the robotics club after their robot broke twice, but Lena remained _____, staying late every Friday until it finally worked.

refute|sc1.stem: Ava insisted that goldfish remember things for only three seconds, but Malik was able to _____ her claim with a study showing goldfish recalled a feeding signal for months.

frenzy|sc2.stem: The classroom was calm all morning, but when the principal announced an early dismissal for snow, the class erupted into a _____ of cheering and backpack-grabbing.
