A chronicle is a written record of events, not a burst of cheering.
A stigma is a mark of shame, but the students were happily cheering.
An early dismissal is not a stage of progress; the class erupted in wild excitement.
The class did not split apart; they all cheered and grabbed backpacks together.
An oasis is a desert water spot, not an outburst of cheering students.

simulate|sc1.stem: Astronauts train in giant swimming pools that _____ the weightlessness of space, letting them practice repairs while floating as they would in orbit.

decoys.why: The pools let astronauts float as in orbit, so they imitate weightlessness rather than resist it.
The pools create the floating feeling of space; they do not hold it back.
The sentence is about copying the feeling of space, not speeding anything up.
The pools help astronauts practice floating, so they recreate weightlessness instead of weakening it.
Nothing is being removed for being unacceptable; the pools copy how space feels.
You cannot cancel weightlessness; the pools imitate it so astronauts can practice.

simulate|sc2.stem: Our science teacher used a fan and a tub of water to _____ a hurricane, creating a tiny version of its wind and waves right on her desk.

decoys.why: She was creating a tiny version of a hurricane, not holding up against one.
The teacher made wind and waves on purpose, so she was not holding the storm back.
She was making a small copy of a hurricane, not speeding one up.
The sentence says she created a tiny version of the storm, not weakened it.
You cannot officially cancel a hurricane; she was making a model of one.

discreet|sc1.stem: Because Olivia had promised to keep her friend's news private, she was _____ when others asked, politely changing the subject without revealing anything.

decoys.why: Olivia was careful to keep the news private, so she was not careless.
The sentence is about keeping a secret, not about being loud enough to hear.
Olivia was keeping a promise politely, not resisting rules or authority.
The clue is that she revealed nothing, not that she expressed ideas clearly.
Olivia was guarding a secret, not longing for the past.
Nothing repeated; the sentence describes Olivia carefully keeping her friend's news private.

discreet|sc2.stem: Unlike his brother, who announced every surprise before the party even started, Leo was _____ and never let a single hint slip about the gift.

decoys.why: Leo never let a hint slip, so he was careful, not careless.
Leo stayed quiet about the gift, so being loud enough to hear does not fit.
The clue is that Leo kept the secret, not that he spoke clearly.
The contrast is about keeping secrets, not about having energy and enthusiasm.
Leo was keeping a surprise, not resisting rules or authority.
The sentence is about not revealing the gift, not about being impossible to defeat.

stringent|sc1.stem: The space agency has _____ cleanliness rules for its labs: workers must wear full-body suits, and even a single speck of dust can halt the work.

decoys.why: Full-body suits and stopping work over one speck of dust show the rules are strict, not loose.
The rules are described openly; the clue is how strict they are.
Rules cannot resist authority; the sentence shows how strict the lab rules are.
Cleanliness might make you think of germs, but rules do not spread from person to person.
The sentence is about strict cleanliness, not about whether rules can be heard.
Lab rules about dust have nothing to do with longing for the past.

stringent|sc2.stem: At home, Nina's bedtime was flexible on weekends, but summer camp had _____ rules: lights out at nine sharp, and counselors checked every cabin.

decoys.why: Lax describes Nina's flexible home bedtime, but camp had lights out at nine sharp.
The rules themselves are strict; rules cannot resist authority.
Counselors checked every cabin openly, so the rules were strict, not secret.
Rules cannot be nervous or upset; the clue is lights out at nine sharp.
Camp rules about bedtime do not long for the past; they are strict.
The sentence contrasts flexible and strict bedtimes, not things happening at the same time.

reputable|sc1.stem: For her science report, Chloe used only _____ sources, such as university websites and well-known encyclopedias, instead of random blogs.

decoys.why: The sources were well-known encyclopedias, not secret or hidden ones.
Chloe avoided random blogs, so her sources were carefully chosen, not careless.
Sources do not spread wildly out of control; the clue is about trust.
University websites do not long for the past; the sentence is about trusted information.
Nothing in the sentence is about timing, only about sources being trusted instead of random.
Websites and encyclopedias are read, not heard, so loudness has nothing to do with it.

reputable|sc2.stem: Because the repair shop had fixed cars honestly for forty years and earned glowing reviews, Mom called it the most _____ garage in town.

decoys.why: The shop worked honestly for forty years, so it was careful, not careless.
A shop with glowing reviews is well known, not secret or hidden.
Forty years is a long time, but a garage does not long for the past.
Honest work and glowing reviews show trust, not resisting rules.
A garage cannot be nervous or upset; the clue is about honesty and reviews.
The sentence praises the shop's honesty, not its size or weight.

artifact|sc1.stem: Among the most valuable items the archaeologists uncovered was a carved clay pot, an ancient _____ that revealed how early farmers stored their grain.

decoys.why: The pot revealed how farmers stored grain, so it explained things rather than being a mystery.
A carved clay pot is an object, not a surprise attack.
A clay pot is not a green spot with water in a desert.
The archaeologists found an object, not a state of anger and disturbance.

artifact|sc2.stem: Jayden thought the rusty spoon he dug up was just junk, but the museum guide explained it was a real _____ used by settlers three hundred years ago.

decoys.why: A spoon is an object people used, not a written record of events.
Jayden thought the rusty spoon was junk, so it was not an impressive sight.
Settlers used the spoon as a tool, not as a mark of shame.
A spoon dug from the ground is an object, not the highest point of something.
Settlers used the spoon, and you cannot use a noisy fight like a tool.
The guide described an old object people used, not a plant disease.

culprit|sc1.stem: When the garden's lettuce kept disappearing overnight, Ming set up a camera and discovered the _____: a chubby rabbit squeezing under the fence.

decoys.why: The lettuce vanished because of a rabbit, not a plant disease.
The camera solved the mystery, so Ming found the one responsible, not a mystery.
A chubby rabbit is not an object made by people long ago.
The garden may feel like one to the rabbit, but the rabbit itself is not an oasis.
The rabbit is the one causing the problem, not a terrible disaster itself.
A rabbit is not a mark of shame; Ming found who was eating lettuce.

culprit|sc2.stem: The muddy paw prints leading from the spilled trash can straight to the dog's bed made it obvious that Biscuit was the _____ behind the mess.

decoys.why: The paw prints made it obvious, so Biscuit was not a mystery.
The mess is a kind of disorder, but Biscuit is the one who caused it.
A spilled trash can is not a terrible disaster, and Biscuit is a dog.
Biscuit is a dog, not an object made by people long ago.
The sentence is about who made the mess, not a desert water spot.
Biscuit caused the mess; a dog is not a mark of shame.

stamina|sc1.stem: Marathon runners need great _____, since they must keep moving for more than twenty-six miles without stopping to rest.

decoys.why: The clue is running twenty-six miles without rest, which takes energy, not fame.
Wild excitement burns out fast, but the sentence is about keeping going for miles.
Special words will not keep you running for twenty-six miles.
Confusion and disorder do not help a runner keep moving without rest.
Anger and disturbance have nothing to do with running a long distance.
Showing respect to someone does not help you run twenty-six miles.

stamina|sc2.stem: Although Ava was the fastest sprinter on the team, she lacked _____ and was always gasping for air halfway through the long cross-country races.

decoys.why: Ava was gasping for air in long races, so she lacked energy, not reputation.
Gasping halfway through a long race shows she ran out of energy, not excitement.
Special words have nothing to do with gasping for air during a race.
The sentence is about getting tired in long races, not showing respect.
Lacking anger and disturbance would not make Ava gasp for air.
Lacking confusion would not explain why she tired out in long races.

resent|sc1.stem: Sofia began to _____ her older brother because their parents always gave him the front seat, even when it was clearly her turn.

decoys.why: Sofia is upset about unfair treatment, not trying to teach her brother something.
She feels cheated out of her turn, so she would not pay her brother back.
Sofia is not imitating her brother; she feels bitter about the front seat.
Nothing is being cut out; the sentence is about her feelings of unfairness.

resent|sc2.stem: Instead of feeling grateful for the extra chores his coach assigned, Marcus started to _____ them, grumbling that the other players never had to stay late.

decoys.why: Marcus was grumbling about the chores, so he was not supporting them.
The coach assigned the chores, so Marcus has no power to cancel them.
The sentence is about how Marcus felt, not combining chores into one.
Marcus was not imitating the chores; he was grumbling that they were unfair.
Grumbling shows bitter feelings, not changing the chores to improve them.

exemplary|sc1.stem: Mr. Ito praised Fatima's _____ science notebook, holding it up so the class could see the neat diagrams and careful notes he hoped everyone would copy.

decoys.why: The notebook has neat diagrams and careful notes, so it is not careless at all.
Mr. Ito held it up for the class to see, so nothing about it was hidden.
He hoped everyone would copy it, so it is a model, not something breaking rules.
Rampant means spreading out of control, which does not describe a neat notebook.
Nothing in the sentence is about missing the past; it is about neat, careful work.
A notebook is not heard; the sentence praises its neat diagrams and notes.

exemplary|sc2.stem: Coach Rivera was frustrated by the team's sloppy passing, but she pointed to Dante's _____ footwork and told everyone to study exactly how he moved.

decoys.why: The coach wants everyone to study Dante's moves, so his footwork is not careless.
Nervous, upset footwork would not be something the coach tells everyone to study.
The coach holds Dante up as a model, not as someone resisting her rules.
Footwork cannot long for the past; the sentence is about how well he moved.
She pointed to his footwork so everyone would watch it, so it was not hidden.
Footwork is not large and heavy; the clue is that others should copy it.

hefty|sc1.stem: The movers groaned as they carried the _____ oak piano up three flights of stairs, stopping every few steps to catch their breath.

decoys.why: Sleek describes a smooth look, but the movers groaning shows the clue is about weight.
Plentiful means many of something, but there is only one piano being carried.
A royal look would not make movers stop every few steps to catch their breath.
The movers groaned from the load, not because of how loud the piano is.
A piano cannot long for the past; the sentence is about how heavy it is.
Being a fine model piano would not make the movers groan on the stairs.

hefty|sc2.stem: Grandpa's old dictionary was so _____ that it made Lily's backpack sag, while her new e-reader weighed less than a sandwich.

decoys.why: The dictionary made the backpack sag, unlike the light e-reader, so it was heavy, not streamlined.
Plentiful means many, but this is one dictionary that is heavy.
It is Grandpa's old book, but the sagging backpack shows the clue is about weight.
Looking royal would not make a backpack sag; the sentence compares weights.
Being trusted does not make a book weigh more than a sandwich.
Dictionaries hold words, but the sentence is about the backpack sagging from weight.

censor|sc1.stem: Before the school newspaper went to print, the advisor would _____ any article containing rude language, blacking out words she considered inappropriate.

decoys.why: She was blacking out words, so she was removing parts, not supporting the article.
The sentence says she blacked out words, which is an action, not just a bitter feeling.
Imitating an article would not explain blacking out words she found inappropriate.
Combining articles is not the same as blacking out rude words in them.
Speeding up an article makes no sense; she was removing words before printing.
You cannot give an article understanding; she was blacking out rude words.

censor|sc2.stem: The library's old policy let leaders _____ books they disliked, but now readers can see every page exactly as the author wrote it.

decoys.why: Now readers can see every page, so the old policy removed parts, not just disliked them.
The contrast is about seeing every page, so leaders removed parts rather than spreading lies.
The old policy hid parts of books leaders disliked, so they were not supporting them.
Imitating books does not contrast with readers now seeing every page as written.
Combining books is not the opposite of seeing every page exactly as the author wrote it.
The contrast is about pages being changed or removed, not about holding books skillfully.

plentiful|sc1.stem: Unlike the dry desert, where food is scarce, the rainforest offers _____ fruit, so monkeys rarely have to travel far for a meal.

decoys.why: The contrast is with scarce food, so the clue is about amount, not heavy fruit.
Monkeys rarely travel far for food, so the fruit is easy to find, not hidden.
Smooth, shiny fruit does not explain why monkeys need not travel far.
Fruit fit for a king does not contrast with food being scarce.
Fruit cannot long for the past; the sentence contrasts scarce and abundant food.
Fruit happening at the same time does not contrast with food being scarce.

plentiful|sc2.stem: After weeks of warm sun and steady rain, tomatoes were so _____ in our garden that we gave bags of them to every neighbor on the street.

decoys.why: Giving bags to every neighbor shows there were many tomatoes, not that they were heavy.
Shiny tomatoes would not explain giving bags of them to every neighbor.
Tomatoes cannot resist rules; the sentence is about having too many to eat.
Being impossible to defeat does not explain giving tomatoes away to the whole street.
The tomatoes were so many you gave them away, not quiet and unnoticed.
Tomatoes are not heard; the clue is that there were too many to keep.

rebellious|sc1.stem: Unlike his obedient sister, Theo was _____, ignoring the camp's lights-out rule and sneaking down to the dock to look at the stars.

decoys.why: Theo is unlike his obedient sister, so he is not deeply loyal to the rules.
He ignored the lights-out rule, so he was not a model camper.
Mild describes weather, and the sentence is about Theo breaking a rule.
Nothing says he missed the past; he was ignoring the camp's rule.
He was sneaking down to the dock, so being loud does not fit.
Being kingly does not contrast with his obedient sister or explain breaking the rule.

rebellious|sc2.stem: After the principal banned hats, a few _____ students wore them anyway, and some even started a petition arguing that the rule was unfair.

decoys.why: These students wore hats against the ban, so they were not model students.
They defied the principal's rule, so they were not loyal to it.
The rule might be strict, but the students were the ones resisting it.
Wearing banned hats and starting a petition is not mild behavior.
The students were fighting a rule they found unfair, not longing for the past.
The sentence is about breaking a hat rule, not about the students' size.

regal|sc1.stem: In her velvet cape and jeweled crown, the actress playing the queen looked truly _____ as she swept grandly across the stage.

decoys.why: She swept grandly across the stage, which shows calm confidence, not nervous upset.
A jeweled crown and a grand sweep across the stage draw attention rather than avoid it.
She is playing the queen, the one in charge, not someone resisting authority.
The sentence describes how royal she looked, not how large or heavy she was.
Nothing in the sentence shows her longing for the past; it describes a royal appearance.
The clues are a cape and crown, which point to royalty, not religion.

regal|sc2.stem: Our scruffy mutt usually looks silly, but after his bath and haircut he sat on the porch with his head held high, looking almost _____.

decoys.why: He sat calmly with his head held high, so he was not nervous or upset.
Sitting proudly on the porch shows dignity, not resisting rules.
The sentence is about how proud he looked, not about missing the past.
A bath and haircut would not make a dog look large and heavy.
Head held high suggests royal pride, not deep religious feeling.
He was sitting quietly, and the sentence is about his proud look, not his opinions.

sleek|sc1.stem: Engineers gave the new train a _____ design, with a glossy, rounded nose that lets it slice through the air at high speeds.

decoys.why: A design that slices through the air at high speed is streamlined, not large and heavy.
The train is new and built for speed, not designed to recall the past.
The glossy, rounded nose is about smooth speed, not looking fit for a king.
Engineers may follow strict rules, but a glossy, rounded nose describes smoothness, not strictness.
The sentence is about a glossy, streamlined shape, not about keeping things hidden.
A train design cannot resist authority; the clues describe a smooth, shiny shape.

sleek|sc2.stem: My old bike was rusty and covered in scratches, but my new one is _____, with glossy black paint and curved lines that gleam in the sunlight.

decoys.why: The clues are glossy paint and curved lines, which describe smoothness, not heaviness.
The sentence contrasts the old bike with the shiny new one, so longing for the past misses.
A bike cannot feel nervous; the clues describe gleaming paint and curved lines.
The sentence describes how the bike looks in the sunlight, not how it sounds.
Paint that gleams in the sunlight draws attention rather than avoiding it.
Glossy paint and curved lines describe appearance, not resisting rules.

devout|sc1.stem: A _____ fan of the team for fifty years, Mrs. Garza had never missed a home game, even during the coldest snowstorms.

decoys.why: Never missing a game for fifty years shows intense loyalty, not a mild interest.
Faithfully attending every game shows loyalty, not resistance.
The sentence is about her loyalty to the team, not her size.
Mrs. Garza is a loyal fan, and nothing suggests she is wild.
The clue is fifty years of never missing a game, which shows loyalty, not royalty.
Sleek describes a smooth, shiny surface, not how loyal a fan is.

devout|sc2.stem: Grandpa is a _____ gardener; while the rest of us stay indoors on rainy mornings, he is outside at dawn caring for his roses, just as he has for forty years.

decoys.why: Gardening at dawn in the rain for forty years shows deep devotion, not mild interest.
Caring for roses faithfully for forty years shows loyalty, not resisting rules.
The sentence is about his dedication to gardening, not his size.
Grandpa carefully tends his roses, which is the opposite of wild.
Nothing describes Grandpa as ugly; the clues show his steady dedication.
Going out at dawn for forty years shows loyalty, not royalty.

temperate|sc1.stem: Unlike scorching deserts and freezing poles, the island has a _____ climate, with gentle summers and winters that are rarely cold.

decoys.why: Gentle summers and mild winters are the opposite of a harsh, strict climate.
The climate is gentle, not wild and extreme like deserts or poles.
The sentence is about mild temperatures, not having a large amount of something.
A climate cannot be large and heavy; the clue is gentle summers and winters.
Gentle summers and rarely cold winters describe mildness, not ugliness.
The sentence contrasts extreme and mild weather, not anything royal.

temperate|sc2.stem: Grandma moved to the coast because its _____ weather, never too hot in July and never too cold in January, let her garden almost all year.

decoys.why: Never too hot and never too cold means calm, steady weather, not stormy and restless.
Weather that is never too hot or too cold is gentle, not wild.
The weather is mild enough to garden all year, not harsh and strict.
The clue is about weather that is never extreme, not about large amounts of something.
Weather good for gardening all year is pleasant, not ugly or distorted.
The sentence is about mild temperatures, not something too strong to defeat.

perish|sc1.stem: Without enough water during the long drought, the farmer feared his young tomato plants would _____ before the autumn rains finally arrived.

decoys.why: Without water during a drought, the farmer fears his plants will die, not follow rules.
Tomato plants cannot work together; the drought means the farmer fears they will die.
The farmer fears the plants dying from lack of water, not stepping in to stop something.
Plants cannot guess; the drought clue tells you the farmer fears they will die.
Without water, plants weaken and die rather than combining into a stronger whole.

perish|sc2.stem: While the sturdy oak survived the forest fire, the young pine trees nearby were not so lucky and began to _____ in the flames.

decoys.why: The pines were not so lucky in the fire, which means they died, not followed rules.
Trees burning in flames are being destroyed, not working together.
The unlucky pines were caught in the fire, not stepping in to stop it.
Trees cannot guess; not so lucky in the flames tells you they were destroyed.
Unlike the surviving oak, the pines were destroyed, not made stronger.

agitated|sc1.stem: As thunder rumbled closer, the horses grew more and more _____, stamping their hooves and pacing nervously around the barn.

decoys.why: The horses were stamping and pacing nervously, so they were not growing mild and calm.
Stamping hooves draws attention, so the horses were not being quiet and careful.
Horses can be sleek, but the sentence describes nervous pacing, not a smooth, shiny coat.
Horses can look regal, but pacing nervously in a storm shows fear, not royal dignity.
The thunder made the horses nervous, not fondly longing for the past.
The sentence is about nervous horses, not horses open to new ideas.

agitated|sc2.stem: Although my little brother usually sleeps calmly through the night, he was _____ before his first day of school, tossing, turning, and asking questions until midnight.

decoys.why: Tossing and turning until midnight is the opposite of being mild and calm.
He was nervous about his first day ahead, not longing for the past.
The sentence shows he could not stay calm, not that he was open to new ideas.
Asking questions until midnight is not quiet or careful to avoid attention.
Tossing and turning all night is not a model of good behavior for others.
The sentence describes nervousness, not being careless or not strict enough.

outspoken|sc1.stem: Unlike her shy brother, who rarely shares his views, Nadia is _____, never hesitating to tell the student council exactly what she thinks.

decoys.why: Nadia never hesitates to say what she thinks, so she is not careful to keep quiet.
Being open to others' ideas is about listening, but Nadia is speaking her own views.
The sentence is about boldly sharing opinions, not simply being loud enough to hear.
Nothing says Nadia is nervous or upset; she just shares her views boldly.
The contrast is with her shy brother, so it is about speaking up, not being famous.

outspoken|sc2.stem: Because Marcus is so _____ about fairness, he stood up in the cafeteria and told the principal that the new lunch rules punished everyone for one person's mistake.

decoys.why: Marcus stood up in the cafeteria and told the principal, which is the opposite of keeping quiet.
Marcus is speaking up about new rules, not longing for the past.
Standing up to tell the principal is bold, not mild or moderate.

nemesis|sc1.stem: For three straight years, Claire had lost the state tennis final to the same player, so beating her _____ this year felt like the greatest victory of her life.

decoys.why: The other player beat Claire fairly in finals; she did not cause a problem or do wrong.
Claire beat a player who had defeated her three years, not her own energy.
The sentence is about beating a long-time opponent, not beating the highest point.
Claire beat a person who kept defeating her, not the way someone behaves.
Nothing says the player is a mystery; she is a rival Claire lost to three times.

nemesis|sc2.stem: Although the two chess players smile and shake hands before every match, each considers the other a _____, since they have battled for the school title five years in a row.

decoys.why: The players battle fairly for a title, so neither is to blame for a problem.
Each player sees the other as a long-time opponent, not an impressive sight.
A rival in chess is not a terrible disaster; they simply compete every year.
A brawl is a fight, but the blank names a person they battle against.
A blight is a plant disease, not a rival chess player.

inflict|sc1.stem: The sudden hailstorm managed to _____ heavy damage on the orchard, denting parked cars and stripping nearly every apple from the trees.

decoys.why: The hail dented cars and stripped the apples, so it caused damage rather than survived it.
A storm does not skillfully hold and use damage like a tool; it causes it.
The damage was real, with dented cars and stripped trees, not imitated.
The hail damaged the orchard right away; it did not put the damage off until later.
The storm caused heavy damage instead of holding it back.

inflict|sc2.stem: The coach warned that a single careless tackle could _____ a serious injury on a teammate, so she made everyone practice safe blocking for a whole week.

decoys.why: The coach fears a tackle causing an injury to a teammate, not surviving one.
The coach worries about a real injury, not a pretend one.
A tackle does not skillfully hold and use an injury; it causes one.
A careless tackle would cause an injury, not hold one back.
The worry is about causing an injury, not putting one off until later.

slander|sc1.stem: Jealous of her success, a rival baker tried to _____ Mrs. Okoye by spreading false rumors that her shop used spoiled ingredients.

decoys.why: Spreading false rumors damages her name; it does not give her knowledge.
The baker spread false rumors about her, not cut parts out of something she said.
The rival already felt jealous; the blank is the action of spreading false rumors.
False rumors about spoiled ingredients tear her down rather than support her.
The rival was spreading lies about her, not imitating how she looks or works.

slander|sc2.stem: Instead of praising the new mayor for fixing the park, the angry letter tried to _____ her, claiming falsely that she had stolen money from the town budget.

decoys.why: The letter made false claims against her instead of praising or supporting her.
The letter spread a false claim about her, not knowledge for her.
The letter is angry, but the blank is the action of making false, damaging claims.
The letter accused her falsely; it did not remove parts of her words.
You revoke a rule or permit, but the letter was making false claims about her.

receptive|sc1.stem: The new principal was _____ to student ideas, listening carefully to every suggestion and even adopting the plan for a school garden.

decoys.why: The principal listened and adopted a student plan, so very strict is the opposite of the clue.
The sentence is about listening to ideas, not about boldly stating her own opinions.
Listening carefully and adopting a plan shows openness, not being nervous and upset.
The principal welcomed ideas, and resisting authority does not describe that at all.
Being fit for a king says nothing about listening to student suggestions.

receptive|sc2.stem: My grandfather usually grumbles about new gadgets, but when I showed him how video calls work, he was surprisingly _____ and asked me to teach him more.

decoys.why: He asked you to teach him more, so he was open, not nervous and upset.
The word surprisingly shows he did not resist the gadget this time, he welcomed it.
Asking to learn more shows openness, not being strict and exact.
His usual grumbling is the habit he broke, so boldly voicing opinions misses the clue.
The sentence is about accepting something new, not about keeping secrets quietly.
Being fit for a king has nothing to do with wanting to learn video calls.

illustrious|sc1.stem: Marie Curie's scientific career was truly _____: she became the first person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

decoys.why: Science can be strict, but two Nobel Prizes point to fame and admiration.
The clue is her prizes and fame, not whether her career was clear to understand.
Being the first to win two Nobel Prizes is anything but mild or ordinary.
Plentiful describes large amounts of things, not a famous and admired career.
Record-setting Nobel Prizes made her famous, the opposite of staying unnoticed.

illustrious|sc2.stem: The violinist had played for presidents and kings for fifty years, so when she visited our small music school, every student lined up to meet the _____ performer.

decoys.why: Students lined up to meet her because she was famous, not because she avoided attention.
Nothing in the sentence says she was upset; it stresses her long, famous career.
Smooth and shiny describes objects, not a performer admired for fifty years of achievement.
Playing for presidents and kings shows fame, not resisting rules.
The clue is her great career, not whether she boldly states her opinions.

pious|sc1.stem: The medieval pilgrims were so _____ that they walked hundreds of miles to visit a holy shrine, praying at every church along the way.

decoys.why: Praying at every church shows deep faith, not resisting authority or rules.
The pilgrims prayed and visited a shrine, which shows religion, not fame.
Being made up would not explain why they walked hundreds of miles to pray.
Their long walk and prayers show devotion, not being nervous and upset.
Pilgrims praying at churches are being religious, not acting like kings or queens.
Being large and heavy does not explain walking far to visit a holy shrine.

pious|sc2.stem: Though her older brother rarely thought about religion, Ana was _____, attending services every week and reading her prayer book each night before bed.

decoys.why: Ana went to services every week, so she followed her faith rather than resisting it.
The sentence describes her quiet prayers and services, not boldly stating opinions.
Reading her prayer book each night shows faith, not nervousness.
Nothing says Ana was famous; the contrast with her brother is about religion.
Weekly services and nightly prayers show deep faith, not something mild.

attentive|sc1.stem: Unlike the students who doodled during the lecture, Marco was _____, taking careful notes and asking thoughtful questions at the end.

decoys.why: Taking careful notes shows focus, not being nervous and unable to stay calm.
Unlike the doodlers, Marco followed the lecture closely, so resisting rules is backward.
He asked questions, but the clue is careful listening and note taking, not bold opinions.
Expecting the worst has nothing to do with taking careful notes.
The sentence is about paying attention in a lecture, not about religion.
Being fit for a king does not contrast with doodling during a lecture.

attentive|sc2.stem: The lifeguard stayed _____ all afternoon; she never looked at her phone and kept her eyes on every swimmer in the crowded pool.

decoys.why: She calmly kept her eyes on every swimmer, which is watchful, not nervous and upset.
Temperate describes mild weather, but the sentence is about her careful watching.
Smooth and shiny might describe a swimmer, but the clue is that she watched everyone.
The sentence never says she expected the worst; it says she kept watching closely.
She did her job carefully all afternoon, so resisting rules is the opposite.

feral|sc1.stem: The kittens had been born in the woods and never handled by people, so they were completely _____, hissing and fleeing from anyone who approached.

decoys.why: The kittens hissed and fled, so being too ready to obey is the opposite.
Fleeing from anyone who approached is the opposite of being open and welcoming.
Cats can be sleek, but the clue is that they were never handled by people.
Nothing says they looked ugly; the sentence describes how wild they acted.
Kittens born in the woods that hiss at people are wild, not royal.
Hissing and fleeing is not mild behavior, and the clue points to wildness.

feral|sc2.stem: Our dog Biscuit sleeps on the couch and loves belly rubs, but the _____ dogs roaming the abandoned farm snarled and bolted whenever a person came near.

decoys.why: The farm dogs snarled and bolted, which is the opposite of obeying people.
Dogs that snarl and run from people are not open or welcoming.
The sentence contrasts tame Biscuit with wild dogs, not smooth or shiny ones.
Size is not the contrast here; the difference is tame versus wild.
Dogs roaming an abandoned farm are wild, not famous for great achievements.

grotesque|sc1.stem: The Halloween mask was truly _____, with a twisted nose, one bulging eye, and a mouth stretched crookedly across its face.

decoys.why: The mask is twisted, bulging, and crooked, which is the opposite of smooth and streamlined.
A twisted nose and crooked mouth do not make a mask look fit for a king.
The sentence describes how ugly the mask looks, not whether it is famous for achievements.
Temperate describes mild weather, and nothing in the sentence is about climate.
Lucid means easy to understand, but the clues describe a strange, distorted face.

grotesque|sc2.stem: In the fairy tale, the princess expected a handsome prince to arrive, but instead a _____ troll with warty skin and a lopsided jaw lumbered out of the forest.

decoys.why: The word instead tells you the troll is the opposite of a handsome prince, not kingly.
Warty skin and a lopsided jaw are not smooth and shiny.
The clues describe the troll's ugly looks, not whether it is religious.
Lucid means clear and easy to understand, which does not describe warty skin.
Temperate describes mild weather, not a troll with a lopsided jaw.

predominant|sc1.stem: Although the forest contains maples, birches, and oaks, pine is the _____ tree, making up nearly three-quarters of all the trunks.

decoys.why: Pine makes up three-quarters of the trunks, so it is everywhere, not hidden away.
Forests can grow in temperate climates, but the clue is about pine being most common.
The sentence counts how many trunks are pine, not whether pine looks royal.
Making up most of the trunks means common, not famous for great achievements.
Feral means wild after being tame, but the clue is about how many trees are pine.
The sentence says nothing about pine looking ugly; it says pine is most common.

predominant|sc2.stem: Because nearly every student in our class speaks Spanish at home, Spanish is the _____ language you hear in the hallway during lunch and recess.

decoys.why: Nearly everyone speaks Spanish, so it is heard everywhere, not hidden away.
Outspoken describes bold people, but the clue is that most students speak Spanish.
The sentence is about how common Spanish is, not how easy it is to understand.
Nothing suggests Spanish sounds harsh; the clue is that nearly every student speaks it.
The clue is about how many students speak Spanish, not about kings or queens.
Students really speak Spanish at home, so it is not a made-up language.

lucid|sc1.stem: Even though the textbook's chapter on electricity confused everyone, Dr. Patel's _____ explanation using water pipes made the idea easy to grasp.

decoys.why: The explanation made the idea easy to grasp, so it was good, not terribly bad.
Using water pipes as a comparison is not making things up; it made the idea clear.
The sentence praises how clear the explanation was, not how harsh it sounded.
The sentence is about the explanation being easy to grasp, not about anyone being upset.
An explanation that is easy to grasp is clear, not famous for great achievements.
The clue is that the idea became easy to grasp, not that the explanation was most common.

lucid|sc2.stem: Mr. Ortiz's directions for the science project were _____; every step was numbered, explained in plain words, and simple enough for a third grader to follow.

decoys.why: Numbered steps in plain words are excellent directions, not very bad ones.
Plain words and simple steps describe clear directions, not harsh or rude ones.
The directions were real and easy to follow, not made up.
The clues show the directions were easy to follow, not the most common.
Nothing about the directions is ugly; the clues say they were simple and plain.
Temperate describes mild weather, but the clue is that a third grader could follow the steps.

revoke|sc1.stem: After Liam was caught driving the golf cart recklessly around the campground, the manager decided to _____ his permission to use it for the rest of the summer.

decoys.why: Liam drove recklessly, so the manager took his permission away instead of keeping it.
Reckless driving would not earn Liam more permission; it got his permission taken back.
The manager is punishing Liam, not revealing his permission for the first time.
Censor means cutting out unacceptable parts of something like a book, not canceling permission.
The manager is not imitating Liam's permission; he is taking it away as punishment.
Combining things into one whole has nothing to do with punishing reckless driving.

revoke|sc2.stem: Last year the city gave the food truck a permit to park downtown, but after dozens of complaints about litter, officials voted to _____ it.

decoys.why: After dozens of complaints, officials would cancel the permit, not support and keep it.
Complaints about litter would not make officials enlarge the permit; they canceled it.
The permit was given last year, so it cannot be revealed for the first time now.
Censor means removing unacceptable parts of a text, not canceling a parking permit.
Officials responding to complaints would not imitate the permit; they would take it back.
There is only one permit, and the complaints point to canceling it, not combining it.

fictitious|sc1.stem: Although many readers believed Sherlock Holmes was a real detective and mailed letters to his London address, he is entirely _____, created by author Arthur Conan Doyle.

decoys.why: Sherlock Holmes is famous, but the clue says he was created by an author, so not real.
Detectives notice details, but the clue is that an author created him.
The sentence contrasts real with created by an author, not clear with confusing.
The sentence is about whether Holmes is real, not whether he lived hidden away.
Being created by an author makes Holmes made up, not royal.
The clue that an author created him points to made up, not most common.

fictitious|sc2.stem: Because the reporter used a _____ name to protect the student's privacy, nobody at school could figure out who had given the interview.

decoys.why: Secluded describes a hidden place, not a fake name used to protect privacy.
A royal-sounding name would not explain why nobody could figure out who the student was.
A clear name would reveal the student, but the name was meant to hide who it was.
The reporter was protecting the student, so the name was fake, not terribly bad.
Using the most common name is not what kept the student's identity a secret.
Nothing in the sentence is about religion; the name was fake to protect privacy.

pessimistic|sc1.stem: Although the weather forecast predicted sunshine, Grandpa remained _____, packing three umbrellas because he was sure the picnic would be rained out.

decoys.why: Grandpa packed three umbrellas, so he was worried, not too satisfied to bother preparing.
Being open to ideas would mean trusting the sunny forecast, but Grandpa ignored it.
Temperate describes mild weather, not a person who expects the picnic to be rained out.
The sentence is about Grandpa expecting rain, not about him boldly stating opinions.
A submissive person would go along with the forecast, but Grandpa refused to believe it.

pessimistic|sc2.stem: After losing the first five games of the season, Maya grew so _____ that she stopped practicing, convinced her soccer team would never win again.

decoys.why: Maya was sure her team would never win, so she was hopeless, not satisfied with herself.
Being attentive means paying close attention, which does not explain why she stopped practicing.
The sentence says she expected only losses, not that she was open to new ideas.
Temperate means mild, but Maya's feeling was strong enough to make her quit.
Nothing says Maya stated opinions boldly; the clue is that she expected to keep losing.

submissive|sc1.stem: In a wolf pack, the younger wolves act _____ toward the leader, lowering their heads and tails to show that they accept its authority.

decoys.why: Wolves can be wild, but lowering heads to accept authority shows obedience, not wildness.
Regal fits the leader, but the younger wolves are lowering their heads to obey.
Lowering heads and tails is a gentle, obedient act, not a harsh one.
The leader is the strongest; the younger wolves are accepting its authority instead.
Wolves bowing to a leader are not famous for great achievements; they are obeying.

submissive|sc2.stem: Unlike her bold older sister, who argued with every rule, Lila was quiet and _____, doing exactly what the babysitter said without a word of complaint.

decoys.why: Lila did what she was told without complaint, so she was not harsh at all.
A wild child would not do exactly what the babysitter said.
Quiet does not mean hidden away; the clue is that she obeyed without complaint.
Acting like a queen does not match doing exactly what someone else tells you.
The sentence is about Lila obeying, not about her expecting bad things to happen.

jargon|sc1.stem: The computer technician's explanation was so full of _____ like "bandwidth throttling" and "DNS cache" that Grandma could not understand a single sentence.

decoys.why: Grandma was confused, but "bandwidth throttling" is an example of special words, not disorder.
Terms like "DNS cache" are technical words, not energy to keep going.
The examples given are computer terms, not anger and disturbance.
The explanation was full of technical terms, not wild excitement.

jargon|sc2.stem: The science fair judges understood the student's _____ perfectly, but the younger visitors needed her to explain her project again using plain, everyday words.

decoys.why: The judges understood it perfectly, so it was not a mystery to them.
The visitors needed plain words, so the blank is about her words, not her behavior.
Her project was new, and the problem was her special words, not an ancient object.
Explaining again in plain words points to her vocabulary, not her energy.
The fix was using everyday words, so the blank must be about language, not a sight.

enigma|sc1.stem: Scientists still cannot explain how monarch butterflies find the same Mexican forest each winter without ever having been there, so their navigation remains nature's most baffling _____.

decoys.why: Monarchs fly far, but the sentence says scientists cannot explain how they find the forest.
The forest is their destination, but the blank describes their unexplained navigation.
Nothing terrible happens; the butterflies' navigation is baffling, not a disaster.
Baffling and unexplained point to a mystery, not the highest point of something.
Butterfly navigation is not a set of special words used by a group.
The sentence describes something scientists cannot explain, not wild excitement.

enigma|sc2.stem: Our new neighbor never speaks to anyone, leaves only at midnight, and has no name on his mailbox, so to the whole street he is a complete _____.

decoys.why: The neighbor is not anyone's opponent; the street simply knows nothing about him.
He sounds suspicious, but the sentence never says he caused any problem.
He hides from everyone, so he is not an impressive sight; he is a mystery.
The neighbor is strange and unknown, not a terrible disaster.

secluded|sc1.stem: The family rented a _____ cabin deep in the woods, miles from the nearest neighbor and reachable only by a narrow dirt road.

decoys.why: The cabin is deep in the woods, but a building cannot be wild like an animal.
The family actually rented the cabin, so it was real, not made up.
Miles from neighbors describes a hidden place, and a cabin cannot accept new ideas.
A cabin cannot expect the worst; the clue is that it is far from everyone.
A cabin cannot listen or watch; the clues describe how far away it is.

secluded|sc2.stem: Most of the lake's shore was packed with noisy swimmers, but we found a _____ cove behind the rocks where we could read in total quiet.

decoys.why: Most of the shore was crowded, so the quiet cove was not the most common spot.
The cove was quiet and hidden behind rocks, not wild like an animal.
You actually found the cove and read there, so it was real.
A cove cannot be upset, and the sentence describes total quiet and calm.
Behind the rocks and away from swimmers describes a hidden spot, not openness to ideas.

blight|sc1.stem: In the 1840s, a terrible _____ swept through Ireland's potato fields, turning the leaves black and rotting the crops in the ground.

decoys.why: An oasis is a green, healthy spot, but the sentence describes leaves turning black and crops rotting.
A frenzy is wild excitement, not something that rots potato crops in the ground.
An ambush is a hidden surprise attack, not a disease that turns leaves black.
A brawl is a noisy fight between people, and it cannot rot crops.
An enigma is a mystery, but the sentence describes something that killed plants.

blight|sc2.stem: Every elm tree on our street once stood tall and green, but after a _____ spread from tree to tree, workers had to cut down all the dying elms.

decoys.why: A frenzy is wild excitement, and it would not leave elm trees dying.
A brawl is a fight between people, not something that spreads from tree to tree.
A vendetta is a bitter feud, and trees cannot catch one and die.
A proponent is a supporter of an idea, not a sickness that kills trees.

abrasive|sc1.stem: The new coach's _____ manner, with constant shouting and cutting insults, rubbed the players the wrong way until several considered leaving the team.

decoys.why: Shouting and cutting insults are not lovable, so endearing is the opposite here.
A coach who shouts and insults is not too ready to obey others.
Receptive means open and willing, but the coach's insults drove players away.
Temperate means mild, and constant shouting is far from mild.
Attentive is a kind, positive trait, but the players wanted to leave because of his manner.

abrasive|sc2.stem: Unlike the soft cotton towels in the bathroom, the scrubbing pad in the kitchen is so _____ that it can scrape burned food right off a pan.

decoys.why: Temperate means mild, but the pad is rough enough to scrape off burned food.
Being basic would not explain why the pad can scrape burned food off a pan.
The sentence contrasts the pad with soft towels, so it must be rough, not yielding.
Being lovable has nothing to do with scraping burned food off a pan.
Feral describes wild animals, not the rough texture of a scrubbing pad.
Lucid means clear and easy to understand, which does not describe a rough pad.

enlighten|sc1.stem: Confused by the strange symbols on the old map, the travelers asked a local fisherman to _____ them about what each mark meant.

decoys.why: The confused travelers wanted to learn what the marks meant, not to be made less eager.
The travelers wanted an explanation, not false statements that damage their reputation.
Censoring removes information, but the travelers wanted to learn what each mark meant.

enlighten|sc2.stem: Our librarian loves to _____ curious students, and she always explains hard topics until everyone in the room finally understands.

decoys.why: She explains until everyone understands, so she helps students rather than making them less eager.
The librarian loves helping students, so she does not feel bitter toward them.
She explains hard topics kindly, not spreading false things about students.
She gives students more knowledge, while censoring would take information away.

calamity|sc1.stem: The volcanic eruption that buried Pompeii in ash was a _____ for the ancient Romans, destroying the entire city in a single day.

decoys.why: A blight is a plant disease, but this disaster was a volcanic eruption burying a city.
A pinnacle is a high point, but losing an entire city was a terrible low point.
A frenzy is wild excitement, not a disaster that destroys a city in a day.
A brawl is a fight between people, not a volcano burying a city in ash.
A vendetta is a long feud, but the eruption was a sudden natural disaster.

calamity|sc2.stem: Everyone feared the burst pipe would be a _____ that ruined every book in the library, but the janitor shut off the water just in time.

decoys.why: A blight is a plant disease, but the danger here was water ruining books.
Everyone feared the pipe, so they expected a disaster, not a high point.
A frenzy is wild excitement, not water damage that ruins every book.
A brawl is a fight between people, but this was a burst pipe flooding books.
A vendetta is a bitter feud, and a pipe cannot have one.

wield|sc1.stem: The sculptor could _____ a heavy chisel so skillfully that he carved delicate flower petals into the marble without a single crack.

decoys.why: Getting a chisel would not explain how he carved delicate petals so skillfully.
You unveil a finished statue, but here he is using the chisel to carve.
Making the chisel larger has nothing to do with using it skillfully.
He carved with the chisel, so he did not give it up.
He really carved the marble, so he was not just imitating using a chisel.
Censoring removes unacceptable parts of something, not handling a tool with skill.

wield|sc2.stem: At first the new drummer could barely hold his sticks, but after a summer of lessons he could _____ them with the speed and control of a professional.

decoys.why: After lessons he played like a professional, so he did not give up his sticks.
The sentence is about how well he used the sticks, not about getting them.
Revealing the sticks would not show speed and control like a professional.
Making the sticks larger has nothing to do with playing them skillfully.
Putting the sticks off until later would not show professional speed and control.

deplorable|sc1.stem: Inspectors found the old zoo's conditions _____: cages were filthy, water bowls were empty, and several animals were clearly underfed.

decoys.why: Filthy cages and hungry animals are extreme problems, not mild conditions.
Nobody would find filthy cages and underfed animals lovable.
Illustrious means famous and admired, but these conditions earned only disapproval.
The sentence lists dirt and hunger, not anything about being hidden away.
The inspectors actually found these problems, so the conditions were real, not made up.
Distraught describes a person who is upset, not conditions like dirty cages.

deplorable|sc2.stem: Ms. Ortiz praises good sportsmanship, so she called the player's behavior _____ when he shoved an opponent and then mocked him after the game.

decoys.why: Shoving and mocking an opponent is not lovable behavior.
Shoving and mocking someone is aggressive, not too ready to obey.
The sentence is about bad sportsmanship, not about listening or noticing carefully.
Nothing in the sentence is about religion; it is about shoving and mocking.
Ms. Ortiz disapproves of the shoving, so she would not call it admired.
Shoving and mocking have nothing to do with being open to new ideas.

defer|sc1.stem: Because half the team was sick with the flu, the coach decided to _____ the tournament until the following weekend.

decoys.why: Until the following weekend means the tournament still happens later, so it was not canceled.
The coach is delaying the tournament, not revealing it for the first time.
Sick players are a reason to wait, not to make the tournament bigger.
Nothing is being combined; the tournament is moved to the following weekend.
The coach is changing when the tournament happens, not imitating one.
Giving up a claim or belief does not fit moving a tournament to another weekend.

defer|sc2.stem: Maya wanted to answer the hard question right away, but she chose to _____ her reply until she had checked her notes and felt sure.

decoys.why: Maya held back her answer until later instead of showing it right away.
She had not given a reply yet, so there was nothing to take back.
Her reply was not a mistake to fix; she simply waited until she felt sure.
The word until shows she is waiting, not making her reply larger.
She still plans to answer later, so she is not formally giving anything up.
Imitating a reply makes no sense; she is waiting to check her notes.

onslaught|sc1.stem: The moment the new video game went on sale, the company's website crashed under a sudden _____ of millions of eager buyers all trying to order at once.

decoys.why: The crash was a disaster, but the blank names the rush of buyers that caused it.
Millions of buyers crashing a website is a flood, not a peaceful green spot.
The website crashed under a rush of people, not under a highest point.
The sentence is about a sudden flood of buyers, not energy to keep going.
A proponent is one supporter, but the blank needs a huge rush of millions.
No one is being unfairly blamed; millions of buyers rushed in at once.

onslaught|sc2.stem: The goalie stayed calm during the first few shots, but she was soon overwhelmed by an _____ of kicks that her tired team could not stop.

decoys.why: The kicks overwhelmed the goalie by their number, not by being a mystery.
An object from long ago has nothing to do with a flood of shots on goal.
An oasis is a place of relief, but the kicks overwhelmed the tired goalie.
The blank needs a fierce rush of kicks, not an ongoing pain or illness.

unveil|sc1.stem: At the end of the assembly, the art club will _____ its new mural by pulling down the giant sheet that has hidden it for weeks.

decoys.why: Pulling down the sheet shows the whole mural instead of removing parts.
The club pulls down a sheet to show the mural, not to cut it apart.
The mural is shown at the end of the assembly, so nothing is put off.
The club is showing the real mural, not imitating one.
Pulling down a sheet reveals the mural; it does not make it larger.
Pulling down the sheet shows the mural rather than canceling anything.

unveil|sc2.stem: For months the company kept its new phone a secret, but at the big launch event it will finally _____ the design to millions of watching fans.

decoys.why: After months of secrecy, the company will finally show the design, not hide parts.
The word finally tells you the wait is over, not being put off again.
The design was a secret, so there was nothing shown yet to take back.
The company is showing off its own phone, not saying false things about anyone.
The launch event shows the design to fans; nothing is cut off.
The secret is ending at the launch, so the design is being revealed, not enlarged.

demeanor|sc1.stem: Although she was terrified of the audition, Lucia kept a calm, confident _____, smiling at the judges and walking steadily to the piano.

decoys.why: Lucia felt turmoil inside, but the blank describes her calm, confident outside.
Smiling and walking steadily show calm, not wild excitement.
The sentence describes how she looked and acted, not a reputation she earned.
Smiling and walking steadily describe her manner, not energy to last a long time.
Lucia is not arguing with anyone; she is smiling at the judges.
The blank is about how she carried herself, not a highest point.

demeanor|sc2.stem: The new librarian's warm, friendly _____ made shy students feel welcome, since she greeted everyone with a smile and spoke in a gentle voice.

decoys.why: Smiling and a gentle voice describe her manner, not a reputation from achievements.
Smiles and a gentle voice describe her behavior, not special words she uses.
A gentle voice and calm smile are the opposite of wild excitement.
A bitter feud could never be warm and friendly or make students feel welcome.
The librarian is greeting students kindly, not answering an argument.
A fierce attack would scare shy students, not make them feel welcome.

complacent|sc1.stem: After winning their first three games easily, the soccer players became _____ and stopped practicing hard, so they were shocked when they lost the championship.

decoys.why: The players stopped practicing hard, so they were not carefully paying attention.
After easy wins they expected to win, which is why the loss shocked them.
Winning three games easily would not make players extremely upset.
Nothing in the sentence is about obeying others; it is about getting lazy after winning.
Being open to new ideas would not make them stop practicing hard.

complacent|sc2.stem: Unlike her teammates, who relaxed after one good season, Priya never grew _____; she kept training every morning as if she had something to prove.

decoys.why: Priya kept training hard, so saying she never grew attentive makes no sense.
The sentence is about relaxing after success, not about religion.
The teammates relaxed; they did not turn wild, so feral does not match.
The contrast is about relaxing versus working hard, not about being lovable.

augment|sc1.stem: To _____ his small weekly allowance, Ahmed began mowing neighbors' lawns, which nearly doubled the money he had each month.

decoys.why: Ahmed doubled his money, so he was adding to his allowance, not giving it up.
Mowing lawns added money; it did not cancel or take back his allowance.
He earned more money right away, so he was not putting anything off.
Cutting off his allowance would not nearly double his money.
He earned real money, so he was not just imitating an allowance.

augment|sc2.stem: Our class wanted to _____ the garden, adding six new tomato plants and a row of sunflowers to the few herbs already growing there.

decoys.why: The class was adding plants, not removing parts of the garden.
Adding tomatoes and sunflowers makes the garden bigger, not cut apart.
The garden already existed with herbs, so nothing was being shown for the first time.
They planted real plants, so they were not imitating a garden.
Adding new plants is doing something now, not putting it off.

renounce|sc1.stem: To become a monk at the mountain temple, Tenzin had to _____ all of his possessions, giving away his books, his clothes, and even his bicycle.

decoys.why: Tenzin was giving his things away, not getting more of them.
Giving away his books and bicycle makes his possessions fewer, not larger.
He gave everything away rather than combining his things into one group.
The sentence is about giving things away, not about feeling bitter toward them.
He actually gave his things away, so he was not putting anything off.

renounce|sc2.stem: Ben had always insisted that ghosts were real, but after the 'haunted' noise turned out to be a raccoon, he decided to _____ that belief.

decoys.why: The noise was just a raccoon, so Ben would not repeat his ghost belief.
Finding a raccoon weakens his belief in ghosts; it does not make it bigger.
The raccoon proved him wrong, so he would not make his belief stronger.
Ben had always insisted on the belief, so it was not being revealed for the first time.

repulsive|sc1.stem: Most visitors find the corpse flower's smell _____, like rotting meat, yet the stink attracts the flies that help the plant make seeds.

decoys.why: A smell like rotting meat is disgusting, not lovable.
The clue rotting meat tells how the smell feels, not how much of it there is.
The comparison to rotting meat describes a disgusting smell, not the most common one.
Rotting meat describes a disgusting smell, not a basic or simple one.
The stink really attracts flies, so the smell is not made up.

repulsive|sc2.stem: My little brother thinks slugs are cute, but my sister finds their slimy trails so _____ that she shrieks and runs whenever she sees one.

decoys.why: Her brother finds slugs cute, but she shrieks and runs, so she is disgusted.
Slime trails cannot listen or notice anything, and she is running from them.
Shrieking and running show disgust, not that the trails seem basic.
Clear and easy to understand does not explain why she shrieks and runs.
She sees the trails and runs, so they are not hidden away.

rectify|sc1.stem: Realizing he had given the customer the wrong change, the cashier hurried after her to _____ the mistake before she left the parking lot.

decoys.why: The cashier hurried before she left, so he was not putting it off.
He wanted to fix the wrong change, not repeat the mistake.
Hurrying after her was meant to undo the mistake, not make it bigger.
He had already realized the mistake, so he did not need to figure it out.
He wanted to set the change right, not hide or remove anything.

rectify|sc2.stem: Instead of blaming her little brother for the broken vase, Nia chose to _____ the situation by gluing the pieces together and admitting she had bumped the table.

decoys.why: Nia was gluing the pieces together, not cutting them apart.
She glued the vase and admitted the truth right away, not later.
Nia admitted she bumped the table, so she was not hiding anything.
She really fixed the vase and told the truth, not just imitated fixing it.
Gluing pieces sounds like combining, but she was fixing a mistake and admitting blame.

rudimentary|sc1.stem: Isabel's Japanese was still _____ after one month of lessons; she could say hello and count to ten, but she could not yet hold a real conversation.

decoys.why: She could only say hello and count to ten, so her Japanese was not clear and fluent.
She knew only a few words, so her Japanese was not large in amount.
A language cannot feel too satisfied with itself; the sentence describes her early skill level.
Her Japanese was real, just limited to hello and counting to ten.
The sentence is about how basic her Japanese was, not whether it was most common.

rudimentary|sc2.stem: My little brother's drawings of our dog are still _____, just circles and sticks, but my older sister's sketches are so detailed they look like photographs.

decoys.why: The sentence says the drawings are just circles and sticks, which means simple, not plentiful.
Simple circles and sticks are not very important events with big effects.
Circles and sticks are easy to draw, so they do not need great effort.
The drawings show their real dog; the clue is that they are simple, not made up.
Feral describes wild animals, not a child's simple drawings of circles and sticks.
Circles and sticks are simple, not disgusting; the contrast is with detailed sketches.

vendetta|sc1.stem: The rivalry between the two bakeries had grown into a bitter _____ that lasted three generations, with each family refusing even to shop on the other's street.

decoys.why: A nemesis is a person, but the blank names the long feud between two families.
An onslaught is a sudden rush of attack, not something lasting three generations.
An upheaval is a sudden change, but this was a feud lasting three generations.
A rebuttal is one answering argument, not a bitter feud lasting three generations.
A calamity is a disaster, but the sentence describes two families refusing each other for years.

vendetta|sc2.stem: Most playground arguments end by lunchtime, but the _____ between Max and Leo lasted all through middle school, with neither boy willing to forgive the other.

decoys.why: A nemesis is one person, but the blank names something between Max and Leo.
A rebuttal is one reply in an argument, not a grudge lasting all of middle school.
An onslaught is a sudden fierce attack, not an unforgiving feud lasting years.
A frenzy is wild excitement, but the sentence describes two boys refusing to forgive.
An upheaval is a sudden big change, not a long grudge between two boys.

procure|sc1.stem: The theater club had to _____ dozens of old costumes for the play, so members spent weeks searching thrift stores and asking neighbors for donations.

decoys.why: Members were searching for costumes to get them, not giving them up.
They spent weeks searching for costumes, so they needed to get them, not reveal them.
They searched thrift stores and asked for donations, so they were getting costumes, not fixing them.
They were not making costumes larger; they were searching to get them.
Searching thrift stores and asking for donations means getting real costumes, not imitating them.
They spent weeks searching for costumes, so they were not putting things off.

procure|sc2.stem: Getting regular tickets was easy, but it took Mia's mom weeks of phone calls to _____ front-row seats; she cheered when the tickets finally arrived in the mail.
