Ms. Fong wants you to avoid these openings, so they must be dull, not friendly.
The contrast with fresh and surprising points to overused, not easily shaped.

trite|sc2.stem: Everyone groaned at the _____ joke about the chicken crossing the road, since they had all heard it at least a hundred times before.

decoys.why: Jokes can be wry, but everyone groaned because they had heard it a hundred times.
A friendly joke wouldn't make people groan; they groaned because it was so overused.
The clue is that everyone had heard it a hundred times, not that it was tricky.
The joke's problem was being heard a hundred times, not being loud.
The sentence says the joke was heard many times, not that it showed early talent.

bravado|sc1.stem: Jason boasted that he wasn't afraid of the haunted house, but his _____ disappeared the moment a skeleton popped out and he ran screaming for the exit.

decoys.why: Ghosts fit a haunted house, but what disappeared was Jason's boastful fake courage.
Jason boasted he wasn't afraid, so what vanished was his bold show, not hand skill.
Jason had no illness; his boasting about not being scared is what vanished.
Future generations make no sense here; the clue is Jason's boast about being unafraid.
Jason wasn't answering an argument; he was boasting, and that fake courage vanished.

bravado|sc2.stem: Ava's _____ before the spelling bee, all that strutting and loud talk about winning easily, was really just a mask for the nervous butterflies in her stomach.

decoys.why: The loud talk was about winning easily before the bee, not a celebration.
Her loud talk was boasting about winning, not an angry speech.
Strutting and talking about winning easily is not a state of not knowing what to do.
Strutting and loud talk about winning describe fake boldness, not skill with the hands.
The sentence describes strutting and boasting, not a messy, disorganized state.
The nervousness is hidden underneath; the blank names the boastful show covering it.

wily|sc1.stem: In the folk tale, the _____ rabbit outsmarted the hungry fox by tricking him into tossing it into the briar patch, exactly where it wanted to go.

decoys.why: The rabbit outsmarted the fox and got what it wanted, so it was not unlucky.
The rabbit cared enough to plan a trick, so it was not uninterested.
The rabbit landed exactly where it wanted, which shows a plan, not randomness.
Trite describes overused phrases or ideas, not a clever rabbit in a story.
Rancid describes spoiled food, and nothing in the sentence is about smell or taste.

wily|sc2.stem: Unlike his honest older brother, who always admitted his mistakes, Jake was _____ enough to blame the broken lamp on the cat and get away with it.

decoys.why: Jake got away with his trick, so he was lucky, not unlucky.
Blaming the cat is sneaky, not stiffly proper behavior.
Being easily shaped by others does not explain cleverly tricking everyone about the lamp.
Trite describes overused ideas, not a boy clever enough to fool his family.
Paltry means meager in amount, which does not describe Jake's sneaky cleverness.

rancid|sc1.stem: The bottle of cooking oil had sat open in the hot garage for a year, so it had turned _____ and gave off a sour, nasty smell.

decoys.why: The clue is a sour, nasty smell, and decrepit means falling apart from age, not spoiled.
Trite means overused and dull, like a phrase, not oil that smells sour.
Shrill describes a sound, but the sentence is about a sour smell.
Raucous describes a loud noise, but the oil gave off a smell.
Gaudy is about showy looks, but the sentence points to a nasty smell.

rancid|sc2.stem: Although the cheese looked perfectly fine on the outside, one sniff told Mom it was _____, so she threw the whole block into the trash.

decoys.why: One sniff told Mom something, so the word must be about smell, not softness.
Bending easily is not something you learn from a sniff.
The cheese looked fine, and gaudy is about looks, while the sniff revealed the problem.
Decrepit means worn out and falling apart, not smelling spoiled.
Mom threw out a whole block, and a sniff shows smell, not a small amount.

obliterate|sc1.stem: The high tide rolled in so powerfully that it managed to _____ every sandcastle on the beach, leaving no trace of the morning's work.

decoys.why: The tide left no trace, which is far more than just weakening the sandcastles.
Dulling the shine would leave the sandcastles standing, but there was no trace left.
The sandcastles were wiped away, not gathered up in a large amount.
Aggravate means make a problem worse, but the tide erased the castles completely.
A tide cannot tease sandcastles; the sentence says it wiped them out.
Formally approving makes no sense for a tide that left no trace of the castles.

obliterate|sc2.stem: Lena thought the rain would only smudge her chalk mural a little, but the downpour went on to _____ it completely, washing every color down the drain.

decoys.why: Lena expected slight damage, but the rain washed away every color, not just dulled it.
The colors washed down the drain, so nothing was being gathered up.
Rain cannot formally approve a mural; the sentence says it washed it away.
Rain cannot tease a mural; the sentence says the colors were washed away.
Questioning has nothing to do with rain washing a chalk mural away.
Forcing with threats makes no sense for rain washing away chalk.

allot|sc1.stem: Since there were only thirty minutes for presentations, Mr. Lee decided to _____ exactly five minutes to each of the six groups.

decoys.why: Mr. Lee is handing out five minutes to each group, not gathering time up.
The sentence is about dividing thirty minutes among groups, not formally approving something.
Mr. Lee is giving out time to each group, not figuring something out by reasoning.

allot|sc2.stem: The art club had only twenty paintbrushes, so Ms. Ortiz had to _____ them carefully, giving exactly two to each table so that no group ran short.

decoys.why: Ms. Ortiz is giving the brushes out to tables, not gathering them up.
She already has the twenty brushes; the sentence is about handing them out.
Destroying the brushes would leave the groups short, the opposite of her goal.
She is giving two brushes to each table, not making them dirty.
The sentence is about sharing the brushes fairly, not dulling their shine.
You cannot question paintbrushes; she is handing them out to tables.

flounder|sc1.stem: When the teacher called on him without warning, Diego began to _____, stammering and flipping through pages because he had not read the chapter.

decoys.why: Diego was stammering and confused, not recovering.
The teacher was questioning Diego, and he was the one struggling to answer.
Diego was not interfering with anyone; he was stammering because he had not read.
Diego is one person, and crowds congregate; he was struggling to answer.

flounder|sc2.stem: Maya glided smoothly across the ice, but her little brother, wearing skates for the first time, could only _____ and grab the wall to stay upright.

decoys.why: Her brother was struggling to stay upright, not recovering from illness.
One boy cannot gather into a crowd; he was struggling clumsily on skates.
He was not interfering with anyone; he was clumsily trying to stay upright.
Questioning someone has nothing to do with wobbling on skates and grabbing the wall.

guile|sc1.stem: Unable to win by strength alone, the small fox in the fable relied on _____, fooling the mighty lion with flattery and a clever lie.

decoys.why: The fox fooled the lion with flattery and a lie, not with a show of boldness.
Flattery and a clever lie are tricks of the mind, not skill with the hands.
The fox won by fooling the lion, and laughter would not trick anyone.
The fox flattered the lion, which is the opposite of showing disapproval.
A clever lie is a careful plan, not a messy, disorganized state.

guile|sc2.stem: The con artist in the movie won the old man's trust through pure _____, pretending to be a long-lost nephew so he could steal the family fortune.

decoys.why: He won trust by pretending to be a nephew, which is trickery, not a show of boldness.
He fooled the man with a false story, not with skillful hands.
The sentence is about a cruel scheme to steal, not about laughter.
Pretending to be a nephew to steal money is a con, not a noisy party.
A con this careful takes planning, not a messy, disorganized state.

beseech|sc1.stem: Desperate to adopt the shivering puppy, the twins dropped to their knees to _____ their mother, pleading over and over until she finally agreed.

decoys.why: The twins dropped to their knees and pleaded, which is begging, not forcing with threats.
The twins were pleading with their mother, not asking her lots of questions.
Kids desperate for a puppy and pleading with their mother do not hate her.
The twins were begging for a puppy, not trying to make their mother feel fresh.

beseech|sc2.stem: Rather than calmly asking for a later bedtime, my little brother chose to _____ our dad, clasping his hands and crying 'please' twenty times in a row.

decoys.why: Clasping his hands and crying please is begging, not forcing with threats.
He kept saying please, which is pleading, not questioning his dad closely.
A boy begging his dad for a later bedtime is not showing hatred.

recuperate|sc1.stem: After the exhausting three-day tournament, the coach gave the players a week off to rest and _____ before practice started again.

decoys.why: A week of rest is meant to make tired players stronger, not weaker.
The players were resting after a tournament, not struggling clumsily.
The week off was for recovering from exhaustion, not for bragging about winning.
The coach gave them time to rest and recover, not to cry softly.
A week off means the players were apart resting, not gathering in a crowd.

recuperate|sc2.stem: Grandpa was pale and weak when he left the hospital, but after a month of good meals and naps he had begun to _____ and was gardening again.

decoys.why: Grandpa was gardening again, so he was getting stronger, not weaker.
Good meals and naps helped him recover, and he was not struggling anymore.
The sentence shows Grandpa getting healthy enough to garden, not crying softly.
Grandpa was recovering his strength, not bragging about anything.
The sentence is about Grandpa regaining his health, not interfering in others' business.

genial|sc1.stem: The _____ shopkeeper always greeted customers with a warm smile, asked about their families, and slipped free candy to the children.

decoys.why: A shopkeeper with a warm smile who gives free candy is not rude or bad-tempered.
He greets customers and asks about their families, so he does not avoid people.
Someone who chats about customers' families does not use very few words.
Asking about families shows he cares, so he is not lacking interest.
His warm smile shows he is cheerful, not sad and lonely.
Nothing in the sentence suggests trickery; he is simply warm and kind.

genial|sc2.stem: Unlike her grumpy older brother, who barely nodded at guests, Mia was _____, chatting happily with every visitor and making sure no one felt left out.

decoys.why: The sentence says Mia is unlike her grumpy brother, so she is not rude.
Mia chats with every visitor, so she is not avoiding people.
Mia chats happily, while her brother is the one who barely speaks.
Mia makes sure no one feels left out, so she clearly cares.
Mia is chatting happily, not sad and lonely.

whimper|sc1.stem: Left alone in the dark hallway, the frightened kitten began to _____ softly, making tiny crying sounds until its owner came home.

decoys.why: A frightened kitten making tiny crying sounds is not bragging.
The sentence describes tiny crying sounds, not clumsy struggling.
The kitten was scared and crying, not recovering from illness.
The kitten was alone making crying sounds, not interfering in anyone's business.

whimper|sc2.stem: The toddler did not scream or throw a tantrum when his balloon floated away; instead he began to _____, his lip trembling as quiet little sobs escaped.

decoys.why: He just lost his balloon and was sobbing, so he was not bragging.
His trembling lip and quiet sobs show sadness, not recovery from illness.
The sentence describes quiet little sobs, not clumsy struggling.
The toddler was crying softly over his balloon, not interfering with anyone.

vagabond|sc1.stem: With no home and no job, the old _____ in the folk tale drifted from village to village, trading songs for bread and a place to sleep.

decoys.why: Nobody is blamed here; the old man simply wanders with no home or job.
A ghost would not need to trade songs for bread and a place to sleep.
An illness might spread between villages, but it cannot trade songs for bread.

vagabond|sc2.stem: Unlike his cousins, who had lived in the same house their whole lives, Uncle Ray had been a _____ in his youth, sleeping in barns and hitchhiking across the country.

decoys.why: Sleeping in barns and hitchhiking shows wandering, not being blamed for others' mistakes.

decrepit|sc1.stem: The _____ old farmhouse had a sagging roof, broken windows, and stairs so rotten that visitors were warned not to climb them.

decoys.why: Prim means neat and proper, but this house has a sagging roof and rotten stairs.
Nothing in the sentence says the house is too bright or showy, only falling apart.
Rancid describes spoiled food, not a house with broken windows and rotten stairs.
Sagging and rotting is decay, not flexibility, so supple does not describe this house.
The sentence describes the house's poor condition, not any loud or harsh sound.

decrepit|sc2.stem: The neighbors had replaced their old bikes with sleek new ones, but Sam still rode his _____ bicycle with its rusty chain and wobbly, bent front wheel.

decoys.why: The bike is rusty and bent, nothing like a too bright, showy bicycle.
The wheel is bent from age and wear, not because the bike is easily shaped.
A wobbly, rusty bike is worn out, not flexible in a good way.
Prim means neat and proper, but this bike has a rusty chain and bent wheel.
Rancid is for spoiled food, not for a rusty old bicycle.

haphazard|sc1.stem: Instead of sorting the donated books by subject, the volunteers had tossed them onto the shelves in a _____ way, so finding any title took ages.

decoys.why: The books were tossed without sorting, which is the opposite of good judgment.
The clue is about no order, not about loud noise while tossing books.
Finding books took ages because of no order, not because anyone was late.
Friendliness does not explain why the books ended up in no order.
Nothing tricky happened; the volunteers just tossed books without any plan.

haphazard|sc2.stem: Because the class planned the field trip in a rush, the schedule was _____: buses arrived late, lunch was forgotten, and nobody knew which group went where.

decoys.why: A rushed plan where lunch was forgotten shows poor judgment, not good sense.
The buses were late, but the schedule itself was disorganized, not late.
The schedule was not flexible; it was a messy, unplanned jumble.
The problem was confusion and no plan, not that the schedule was dull and overused.
Terse describes short, rude speech, not a schedule where nobody knew where to go.

amass|sc1.stem: By saving a little from every birthday and allowance, Keisha was able to _____ over a thousand dollars by the time she turned thirteen.

decoys.why: Keisha was saving money up over time, not giving out shares of it.
She saved a little at a time; she did not dig up hidden money.
Saving builds money up, so destroying it completely makes no sense here.
Saving money does not dull its shine; the sentence is about gathering it.

amass|sc2.stem: Most kids lose interest in rock hunting after a week, but Theo kept going for years and managed to _____ more than five hundred stones from beaches and riverbanks.

decoys.why: Theo was collecting stones for years, not handing out shares of them.
A collector keeps his stones; he does not destroy them completely.
The sentence praises Theo's long collecting, not making stones impure.
Nothing is being covered up; Theo is gathering hundreds of stones.

reclusive|sc1.stem: The _____ artist lived alone on a remote island, refused every interview, and had not attended a public event in over twenty years.

decoys.why: Someone who refuses every interview and lives alone is not friendly and outgoing.
The artist hides away quietly, so loud and harsh does not fit.
The clues are about avoiding people, not about being wildly silly.
Nothing here is about early talent; the clues show the artist avoids people.
A showy person seeks attention, but this artist skips every public event.

reclusive|sc2.stem: Her twin brother loved crowded parties and chatted with everyone, but Nora was so _____ that she spent weekends alone in her room with a book.

decoys.why: That describes her chatty brother; Nora is the one who stays alone.

Being wildly silly would not explain spending weekends alone with a book.
Fearlessness does not explain why Nora avoids people and stays in her room.

terse|sc1.stem: When Zoe asked her brother how his game went, his reply was _____, just a single grumbled "Fine" before he shut his bedroom door.

decoys.why: He grumbled one word and shut his door, which is the opposite of friendly and cheerful.

Nothing about a grumbled "Fine" and a shut door is wildly silly or funny.
The sentence is about how short and rude his reply was, not about good judgment.
One grumbled word is not random or disorganized; it is just very short.

terse|sc2.stem: Usually Grandpa tells long stories at dinner, but tonight his answers were _____, just a nod or a quick "Yep" before he went back to eating.

decoys.why: The sentence contrasts his usual long stories with tonight's nods, not with friendliness.
A nod or a quick "Yep" is quiet, not loud and harsh-sounding.

The clue is that his answers were very short, not that they were random.

zany|sc1.stem: Our science teacher is famous for her _____ demonstrations, like wearing a rubber-chicken hat while launching marshmallows from a homemade catapult.

decoys.why: A rubber-chicken hat and marshmallow catapult are unusual, not dull and overused.
Wearing a rubber-chicken hat is the opposite of quiet, shy, and modest.
The example shows silliness, not careful good judgment.
Nothing in the sentence says the demonstrations are old or falling apart.
Demonstrations are not described by how few words they use; the example is about silliness.

zany|sc2.stem: My older cousin acts calm and serious at work, but at family parties he turns _____, juggling dinner rolls and dancing like a chicken.

decoys.why: Juggling rolls and dancing like a chicken is not quiet, shy, or modest.
The sentence says he stops being calm and serious, so sensible judgment is backwards.
The clue is silly juggling and dancing, not speaking in very few words.
He is performing for everyone at the party, not avoiding people.
Juggling and dancing show silliness, not being old and in poor condition.

shirk|sc1.stem: Whenever it was his turn to clean the hamster cage, Owen tried to _____ the job by suddenly claiming he had a stomachache.

decoys.why: Faking a stomachache is a way to avoid the job, not to hand out shares of it.

Claiming a stomachache does not dig up or discover the job; it dodges it.
A fake stomachache is an excuse to escape the chore, not to make it fresh.
The sentence is about avoiding a chore, not proving someone right or innocent.

shirk|sc2.stem: Unlike her twin, who always finds an excuse to _____ his chores, Mia finishes hers right after school without being asked.

decoys.why: The twin finds excuses to avoid his chores, unlike Mia, not to hand them out.
Mia does her chores while her twin avoids his; judging their value is not the contrast.

Excuses are for getting out of chores, not for making them fresh and lively.
The contrast with Mia shows he avoids chores, not that he digs them up.

abhor|sc1.stem: Nora happily eats broccoli and spinach, but she has always seemed to _____ Brussels sprouts, gagging at even the smell of them cooking.

decoys.why: She gags at the smell, so she would not gather a large amount of them.
Gagging at the smell shows strong hate, not judging their quality.
The clue is her gagging, which shows hatred, not digging up sprouts.
The sentence is about how much she hates sprouts, not making them fresh again.
Gagging at the smell shows hate; it has nothing to do with proving something right.

abhor|sc2.stem: Because my parents _____ loud alarm clocks, they wake up to soft music instead of the harsh beeping that used to make them jump.

decoys.why: They switched to soft music, so they would not collect loud alarm clocks.
They replaced the clocks because the beeping made them jump, not because they judged their value.
The harsh beeping made them jump, which explains hating the clocks, not digging them up.
Switching to soft music shows they hate the beeping, not that they proved the clocks right.
The clue is that the beeping bothered them, not that they handed out alarm clocks.

unkempt|sc1.stem: After a week of camping without showers or a mirror, Noah came home looking _____, with tangled hair, a scruffy face, and wrinkled clothes.

decoys.why: Camping might sound brave, but the clue describes his messy hair and clothes.
The sentence describes his tangled hair and scruffy face, not a friendly mood.
Nothing about tangled hair and wrinkled clothes means easily shaped or changed.
The clue is his messy appearance, not whether he showed good judgment.

unkempt|sc2.stem: Grandma's garden was always neatly trimmed, but after she moved away, the yard grew _____, with weeds and overgrown bushes everywhere.

decoys.why: The yard is full of weeds because no one cares for it, not easily shaped.
An overgrown, weedy yard shows nobody is taking care of it, not good judgment.
A yard cannot be friendly; the clue is the weeds and overgrown bushes.
The sentence contrasts neatly trimmed with weedy, so the blank is about messiness, not modesty.

unearth|sc1.stem: While digging in the school garden, the second-graders were thrilled to _____ an old glass bottle that had been buried there for a century.

decoys.why: The kids were thrilled to find the bottle, not to destroy it completely.
The bottle was already buried, and digging uncovers things rather than covering them up.
Dulling a bottle's shine has nothing to do with digging it up from the garden.
Nothing in the sentence is about making the bottle dirty or impure while digging.
The kids were thrilled, so they would not hate the bottle they found.

unearth|sc2.stem: After weeks of reading old newspapers in the library, the student reporter managed to _____ a long-forgotten secret about who had founded our town.

decoys.why: Weeks of research bring a secret to light; they do not cover it up.
The reporter was reading to discover the secret, not to wipe it out.
You prove a person right, but the reporter was finding a forgotten secret.
Tarnish can mean damage a reputation, but the reporter found a secret through research.
You amass a large pile over time, not one single forgotten secret.

tardy|sc1.stem: Because the bus broke down on the highway, half the class was _____ and missed the first ten minutes of the morning quiz.

decoys.why: The broken bus might be decrepit, but the students were late because of it.
The class missed the quiz because the bus broke down, not because they didn't care.
Being loud would not make the class miss the first ten minutes of the quiz.
Looking messy does not explain missing the start of the quiz after a breakdown.
A broken bus makes students late, not random or disorganized.

tardy|sc2.stem: Although Jaden usually arrives at soccer practice ten minutes early, he was _____ on Saturday, jogging onto the field after warm-ups had already ended.

decoys.why: The clue is that he arrived after warm-ups ended, which is about time, not good sense.
Being friendly has nothing to do with jogging in after warm-ups had ended.
The sentence is about when he arrived, not about how messy he looked.
Nothing silly happens; he simply showed up after warm-ups were over.
Arriving after warm-ups ended shows lateness, not fearlessness.

dauntless|sc1.stem: Despite freezing winds and two failed attempts, the _____ explorer refused to give up and finally reached the South Pole on her third try.

decoys.why: She refused to give up, so she cared a lot rather than showing no interest.
The sentence praises her refusal to quit, not her sadness or loneliness.
Taking three tries does not make her late; the clue is that she never gave up.
She refused to give up, so she was not easily bent or changed.
A worn out, broken down explorer would not push through freezing winds to the Pole.

dauntless|sc2.stem: Because she was completely _____, the young firefighter rushed into the smoky building to rescue the trapped puppy while others stood frozen in fear.

decoys.why: She rushed in to save a puppy, so she clearly cared a great deal.
She rushed in while others froze, so she was quick, not late.
Others were frozen in fear while she acted, so the blank means brave, not sad.
Careful good sense would not explain rushing into smoke while others stood frozen.
Being friendly does not explain charging into a smoky building when others were afraid.

judicious|sc1.stem: Instead of spending her whole budget on the first costume she saw, Esme made a _____ choice, comparing prices at three stores before buying.

decoys.why: Esme compared prices at three stores, so her choice was planned, not random.
The sentence is about how carefully she shopped, not about a showy costume.
Costumes can be silly, but comparing prices describes a sensible choice.
Comparing prices shows careful thinking, not that her choice came too late.
Her choice was careful because she compared prices, not dull from overuse.

judicious|sc2.stem: Since the hiking trail was icy and the sun was setting, our guide made the _____ decision to turn back early rather than risk a dangerous climb in the dark.

decoys.why: A fearless guide would push on, but this guide wisely turned back from danger.
The guide weighed the ice and sunset, so the decision was not random.
Turning back to avoid danger shows the guide cared about everyone's safety.
Avoiding a dangerous climb in the dark is a sensible decision, not a silly one.
The sentence says they turned back early, so the decision was not late.

rejuvenate|sc1.stem: The town hoped to _____ its run-down park by planting new flowers, repairing the old fountain, and adding a colorful playground.

decoys.why: Planting flowers and fixing the fountain improves the park rather than destroying it.
New flowers and a colorful playground brighten the park, not dull it.
Repairing the fountain fixes damage; corrode means wearing things away.
Planting flowers and repairing things make the park better, not impure.
The town was fixing up the park, not just judging how much it was worth.

rejuvenate|sc2.stem: Dad trudged in from his double shift looking gray and worn out, but a hot shower and a bowl of soup seemed to _____ him, and soon he was laughing with us.

decoys.why: Soon Dad was laughing, so the shower and soup made him feel better, not worse.
A shower and soup that leave Dad laughing did not cover him up.
Nobody forced Dad with threats; the shower and soup refreshed him.
Dad went from worn out to laughing, which is about energy, not being proven right.
Soup cannot judge Dad's value; the clue is that he went from tired to laughing.

pliable|sc1.stem: The craft wire is _____ enough to twist into animal shapes with bare hands, yet it holds its form once you finish bending it.

decoys.why: Languid describes a slow, tired person, not wire you can twist into shapes.
Unkempt means messy, but the sentence is about wire bending easily in your hands.
Haphazard means random, which says nothing about wire being easy to bend.
Animal shapes sound silly, but the wire itself must bend easily, not be funny.
Terse describes speech with few words, not wire you twist with bare hands.
Genial means friendly, but the sentence needs a word for wire that bends easily.

pliable|sc2.stem: Dry modeling clay cracks when you press it, but after a few minutes in your warm hands it becomes soft and _____ enough to shape into a dragon.

decoys.why: Languid fits a tired person, not clay that has softened enough to shape.
Warm hands sound friendly, but the clay must become easy to shape, not cheerful.
Decrepit means falling apart, like the dry clay that cracked, not the softened clay.
A dragon can be fun, but the clay must become easy to mold, not silly.
Soft might suggest quiet and shy, but the clay needs to be easy to shape.
Unkempt means messy and uncared for, which does not explain clay you can shape.

mirth|sc1.stem: The class had been gloomy all week, but the comedian's assembly show filled the auditorium with _____, and students were still giggling at lunch.

decoys.why: Students were giggling all through lunch, so the show brought laughter, not disapproval.
A comedian may act bold, but giggling students show the room was full of laughter.
Guile is trickery, but the giggling students point to amusement and laughter.
Dexterity is hand skill, but the sentence is about students laughing at a funny show.

mirth|sc2.stem: When my baby sister sneezed so hard that spaghetti flew onto Dad's glasses, the whole table was full of _____, and we laughed until our stomachs hurt.

decoys.why: Spaghetti on Dad's glasses might seem rude, but we laughed, so there was no disapproval.
Bravado is fake boldness, but the table was laughing until stomachs hurt.
Nobody was tricking anyone; the sneeze made everyone laugh.
Flying spaghetti shows no hand skill; the sentence says everyone laughed.

gloat|sc1.stem: Coach reminded the team that after a victory they should shake hands politely rather than _____ about the score in front of the disappointed players.

decoys.why: The team won, so the worry is bragging, not crying softly about the score.

gloat|sc2.stem: Max began to _____ about his spelling bee win, so by Friday none of his classmates wanted to sit with him at lunch.

decoys.why: Max won the spelling bee, so he was bragging, not crying about it.

vehement|sc1.stem: Liam was _____ in his opposition to cutting the music program, pounding the podium and speaking with fiery passion at the school board meeting.

decoys.why: Pounding the podium with fiery passion is the opposite of quiet and shy.
Fiery passion and pounding the podium show energy, not slow relaxation.
Liam was fiercely opposing the cut, not acting friendly and cheerful.
The clues stress fiery passion and pounding, not calm good judgment.
Liam was not sorry for anything; he was passionately arguing against the cut.
Speaking loudly at a public meeting is the opposite of secretive.

vehement|sc2.stem: Most students only shrugged when the cafeteria removed pizza from the menu, but Aria was _____ in her complaints, writing three angry letters to the principal.

decoys.why: Writing three angry letters is the opposite of quiet and modest.
Unlike the shrugging students, Aria put lots of energy into her complaints.
Her letters were angry, so she was not friendly and cheerful.
Aria was not sorry; she was angry about the pizza being removed.
Three angry letters about pizza show strong feeling, not careful good judgment.

quandary|sc1.stem: Invited to her best friend's birthday party and the regional chess final on the same afternoon, Keiko was in a real _____ about which to attend.

quandary|sc2.stem: The math problem put Devon in a _____: he could not decide whether to start over or keep checking his messy work, and the clock kept ticking.

decoys.why: Devon could not decide what to do; nothing says he gave an angry speech.

demure|sc1.stem: On stage the singer was loud and flashy, but at home she was quiet and _____, preferring to read alone rather than attract attention.

decoys.why: The sentence contrasts her loud stage self with a quiet home self, and zany means wildly silly.
She is quiet and avoids attention at home, so strong, forceful feeling does not fit.
Nothing in the sentence suggests rudeness; it describes her as quiet and avoiding attention.
Being fearless has nothing to do with preferring to read alone instead of attracting attention.

demure|sc2.stem: The new student was so _____ that she kept her eyes down, spoke softly, and blushed whenever the teacher praised her work in front of everyone.

decoys.why: She keeps her eyes down and speaks softly, which is the opposite of wildly silly.

A fearless student would not keep her eyes down and blush when praised.

fallible|sc1.stem: Although many people trust calculators completely, the math teacher reminded the class that machines are _____ too, since one mistyped number produces a wrong answer.

decoys.why: The teacher says machines give wrong answers, so showing good judgment is the opposite point.

Machines being fearless does not explain why one mistyped number gives a wrong answer.

fallible|sc2.stem: Since even expert weather forecasters are _____, Coach always keeps a backup plan ready in case the predicted sunny day turns into a sudden thunderstorm.

decoys.why: Coach needs a backup plan because forecasts can be wrong, not because forecasters show good sense.
Forecasters being fearless would not make Coach need a backup plan.
Friendly forecasters give no reason to worry that a sunny prediction might be wrong.

Strong feeling has nothing to do with a predicted sunny day turning stormy.

malady|sc1.stem: Centuries ago, sailors on long voyages often suffered from scurvy, a _____ caused by a lack of vitamin C that made their gums bleed.

malady|sc2.stem: The mysterious _____ spread quickly through the chicken coop, and within a week half the hens had stopped laying eggs and were too weak to stand.

decoys.why: Mysterious sounds ghostly, but the hens grew weak and stopped laying, which points to sickness.

impertinent|sc1.stem: When the substitute asked the class to settle down, Brady gave a truly _____ reply, asking whether she even knew how to teach, and was sent straight to the office.

impertinent|sc2.stem: Unlike her younger brother, who often made _____ remarks to their grandparents, Lila always said please and thank you and listened politely at dinner.

decoys.why: The brother is contrasted with polite Lila, so his remarks were not friendly and cheerful.
Unlike polite Lila, the brother's remarks were rude, not wise and sensible.

The contrast is with Lila's politeness, so sorry remarks would not make sense.

languid|sc1.stem: On the hottest afternoon of the summer, the lions lay _____ in the shade, barely lifting their heads even when the zookeeper brought their food.

decoys.why: The lions barely lifted their heads, which is the opposite of wild and full of energy.
Lions may seem fearless, but the clue is that they barely moved in the heat.
Lying in the shade barely lifting their heads shows no strong, forceful feeling.
Wildly silly does not match lions too hot and tired to lift their heads.

languid|sc2.stem: At recess the twins raced around the playground nonstop, but by the end of the long, sticky afternoon they moved in a _____ way, dragging their feet to the bus.

decoys.why: That fits recess, but the word but tells you they later dragged their feet.
Dragging their feet to the bus shows tiredness, not wild silliness.
Kids dragging their feet show no strong, forceful feeling.
Being fearless has nothing to do with being worn out after a long, sticky afternoon.
The clue is dragging their feet, which means slow and tired, not random.
Good judgment does not describe kids too tired to lift their feet.

vindicate|sc1.stem: Everyone laughed at Aiden's claim that the old map showed a hidden creek, but the surveyors' discovery of the stream would later _____ him completely.

decoys.why: Finding the stream proved Aiden right, so it would not scold him.

The surveyors uncovered the stream, but they did not dig up Aiden himself.

vindicate|sc2.stem: When the security camera footage showed a raccoon tipping over the trash cans, it helped _____ our dog, who had been blamed for the mess all week.

decoys.why: The footage showed a raccoon did it, so it cleared the dog instead of scolding him.
The video proved the dog innocent, so it would not lead anyone to reject him.
The sentence is about clearing the dog's name, not making him angry.
The footage cleared the dog of blame; it did not make him feel young again.

appraise|sc1.stem: Before selling Grandpa's coin collection, the family hired an expert to _____ it so they would know how much each coin was really worth.

decoys.why: Grandpa already gathered the coins; the expert was hired to judge their worth.

appraise|sc2.stem: Rather than simply guessing which used bike was the better deal, Dad asked the mechanic to _____ both, carefully judging their brakes, tires, and gears before he decided.

decoys.why: The mechanic was judging the brakes and tires, not fixing the bikes up.

revelry|sc1.stem: The sounds of _____ drifted from the town square all night, as people danced, sang, and set off fireworks to celebrate the harvest festival.

decoys.why: People were dancing and singing to celebrate, so the sounds were of celebration, not messiness.

revelry|sc2.stem: The library was usually hushed, but after our team won the state spelling bee, the _____ in the study room grew so loud that the librarian asked us to quiet down.

furtive|sc1.stem: Hoping no one would notice, Bella stole a _____ look at her phone under the desk while the teacher's back was turned.

decoys.why: Bella hoped no one would notice, so her look was sneaky, not forceful.

furtive|sc2.stem: Unlike his brother, who grabbed snacks openly, Marcus made _____ trips to the kitchen at night, tiptoeing past his parents' door so the floor would not creak.

contrite|sc2.stem: Instead of making excuses for forgetting her best friend's birthday, Nora was genuinely _____, admitting her mistake and baking a cake to make up for it.

spurn|sc2.stem: Because Jordan had teased her all year, Mia decided to _____ his invitation to the party, tossing the card in the trash with a roll of her eyes.

credulous|sc2.stem: While her older sister instantly saw through the prank, _____ little Rosa really believed the cat had learned to talk.

peevish|sc2.stem: My sister is usually sweet and patient, but after a long day at summer camp she turns _____, snapping at anyone who asks her a simple question.

decoys.why: Beaches buried in trash would upset turtle lovers, not make them happy and excited.

The photos show a disgusting mess; they do not prove anyone right or innocent.
Photos cannot hate people; the people would hate what the photos show.
Photos do not judge the value of people who care about sea turtles.

appall|sc2.stem: The guests expected a tasty meal, but the moldy bread and the hair in the soup were enough to _____ even the least picky eaters at the table.

decoys.why: Moldy bread and hair in soup would disgust guests, not make them happy and excited.
The food cannot hate the eaters; the eaters would be disgusted by the food.
Moldy bread cannot wear away eaters by chemical action; it shocks and disgusts them.
The food does not judge the value of the eaters; it disgusts them.
Bad food proves nobody right or innocent; the guests expected a tasty meal.

exhilarate|sc1.stem: Sledding down the steepest hill in town never failed to _____ the twins, who shrieked with joy all the way to the bottom.

decoys.why: The twins shrieked with joy, so the sledding thrilled them rather than disgusted them.
The twins shrieked with joy, not anger, all the way down the hill.
A sled ride cannot scold anyone; the twins were shrieking with joy.
Sledding did not warn or scold the twins; it filled them with joy.
Sledding cannot hate the twins, and the twins clearly loved the ride.
The ride proved nothing; the clue is that the twins shrieked with joy.

exhilarate|sc2.stem: Long car rides usually bore my little brother, but the first glimpse of the ocean through the window seemed to _____ him, and he bounced in his seat cheering.

decoys.why: He bounced in his seat cheering, so the ocean delighted him rather than disgusted him.
He was cheering, which shows excitement, not anger.
The ocean view cannot scold him; it made him bounce and cheer.
The ocean did not reject him; seeing it made him cheer happily.
The ocean cannot hate him, and his cheering shows he loved seeing it.
Seeing the ocean proved nothing; the clue is his excited bouncing and cheering.
